text: 1. The whole position and the whole apparatus of the impious and sacrilegious Marcion we now summon to his very own gospel, which by interpolating he made his own. And in order to furnish it with credit, he devised a sort of dowry for it, a work entitled Antitheses from the oppositions of contraries, and forced into a separation of law and gospel — by which, dividing two gods, accordingly diverse, the one of one instrument, or, what is more usual to say, of one testament, and the other of the other, he might thereafter give patronage to the gospel too, believed in according to the Antitheses. But these I would have struck down by a direct hand-to-hand engagement, that is, through each separate thrust of the man of Pontus, had they not been far more conveniently beaten back in the gospel itself and along with the gospel for whose sake they are contrived; although it is so easy to meet them with a preliminary objection — and indeed in such a way that I accept them, that I ratify them, that I say they work with us, so that they may the more blush for the blindness of their own author — that now the Antitheses are ours against Marcion. And indeed I confess that one order ran its course in the old arrangement with the Creator, another in the new with Christ. I do not deny that the evidences of utterance differ, the precepts of virtue, the disciplines of the law, provided only that the whole diversity converges upon one and the same God — him, namely, by whom it is established to have been arranged just as it was also foretold. Long ago Isaiah proclaims that a law would go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem — another law, surely, and another word. In short, "He shall judge," he says, "among the nations, and shall convict a numerous people" — namely not of the single nation of the Jews, but of the nations, who through the new law of the gospel and the new word of the apostles are judged and convicted in themselves of their former error, as soon as they have believed, and thereupon "beat their swords into ploughshares, and their pikes" (which is a kind of hunting-spear) "into pruning-hooks" — that is, they convert their once fierce and savage spirits into upright senses and into workers of good fruit. And again: "Hear me, hear me, my people, and you kings, give ear to me; for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgement for a light of the nations" — by which he had judged and decreed that the nations too were to be illumined through the law and the word of the gospel. This will be the law also with David, "blameless," because perfect, "converting the soul" — surely from idols to God. This will be also the word concerning which the same Isaiah says: "For the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth." For the new testament has been abridged and freed from the burdensome trappings of the law. But why say more, when novation is proclaimed by the Creator through the same prophet more plainly and more clearly than the light itself? "Remember not the former things, and consider not the things of old: the old things have passed away, new things arise: behold, I make new things, which shall now arise." Likewise through Jeremiah: "Make for yourselves a new freshness, and sow not among thorns, and be circumcised in the foreskin of your heart." And elsewhere: "Behold, the days shall come, says the Lord, and I will perfect for the house of Jacob and the house of Judah a new testament, not according to the testament which I arranged for their fathers in the day when I took hold of their arrangement to lead them out of the land of Egypt." So far does he signify the former testament to be temporary, while he shows it to be changeable, even while he promises an eternal one for the future. For through Isaiah, "Hear me and you shall live, and I will arrange for you an everlasting testament," adding "the holy and faithful things of David," that he might show that testament was to run its course in Christ. The same Christ, descended from the stock of David, according to the registration of Mary, he was also foretelling figuratively in the rod to come forth from the root of Jesse. Therefore, if he said that other laws and other words and new arrangements of the testaments were to come to be from the Creator — so that he even appointed other and preferable offices of the very sacrifices, and that indeed among the nations, Malachi saying, "I have no will in you, says the Lord, and your sacrifices I will not receive from your hands; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, even a clean sacrifice" — namely simple prayer from a pure conscience — it is of necessity that every change coming from innovation should incur a diversity with those things of which it is made, and a contrariety from the diversity. For just as nothing is changed which is not made diverse, so nothing is diverse which is not made contrary. Therefore the contrariety from diversity will be reckoned to belong to the same one whose was the change from innovation. He who arranged the change, the same instituted the diversity too; he who proclaimed the innovation, the same foretold the contrariety too. Why do you interpret the difference of things into a distance of powers? Why do you twist the Antitheses of examples against the Creator, which you can recognize even in his very feelings and affections? "I," he says, "will strike, and I will heal: I," he says, "will kill, and I will make alive" — making evil things, namely, and working peace; by which indeed you are wont to reproach him under the name even of mobility and inconstancy, as forbidding what he commands and commanding what he forbids. Why, then, did you not reckon the Antitheses too among the natural properties of a Creator always contrary to himself? You could not even have considered the world — unless I am mistaken, even among the Pontic peoples — except as built up out of diversities of mutually rival substances. First, then, you ought to have determined one god of light, another of darkness, that so you might be able to assert one of the law, another of the gospel. But it has been judged beforehand from manifest things, that of whom the works and characters are established through the Antitheses, of the same form are established his sacraments too.

2. You have now the answer we have made ready to the Antitheses. I pass now to the demonstration of the gospel — not, to be sure, a Jewish one, but a Pontic, and for the present adulterated — which is to furnish beforehand the order I am approaching. We lay it down first of all that the evangelic instrument has the apostles for its authors, on whom this charge of promulgating the gospel was imposed by the Lord himself. If it has also apostolic men, yet not them alone, but with the apostles and after the apostles — since the preaching of disciples might be made suspect of a passion for glory, if there did not stand by it the authority of their masters, nay of Christ, who made the apostles masters. In short, John and Matthew instil faith into us from the apostles, Luke and Mark renew it from the apostolic men — beginning from the same rules, so far as concerns the one God the Creator, and his Christ, born of a virgin, the supplement of the law and the prophets. For let it be his own concern if the arrangement of the narratives has varied, provided there is agreement on the head of the faith, on which there is no agreement with Marcion. On the contrary, Marcion ascribes to his gospel, namely, no author — as though it had not been lawful for him to fix on it a title too, for whom it was no wickedness to overturn the very body. And here I might already plant my foot, contending that a work is not to be acknowledged which does not raise its forehead, which presents no constancy, which promises no faith from the fullness of a title and the due profession of an author. But we prefer to engage at every point, nor do we conceal what can be understood from what is ours. For out of those compilers whom we have, Marcion seems to have chosen Luke as the one to mangle. Now Luke was not an apostle but an apostolic man, not a master but a disciple, certainly lesser than his master, surely as much later as the follower of a later apostle, of Paul without doubt — so that, even if Marcion had brought in his gospel under the very name of Paul, that single instrument, destitute of the patronage of predecessors, would not suffice for faith. For there would be demanded that gospel too which Paul found, to which he gave credence, with which he soon strove to make his own agree — seeing that for that very reason he went up to Jerusalem to become acquainted with the apostles and to consult them, lest perchance he had run in vain, that is, lest he should not have believed according to them and should not evangelize according to them. In short, when he conferred with the authors and agreed upon the rule of faith, they joined right hands, and thereupon distinguished their offices of preaching, that they should go to the Jews, Paul to the Jews and to the nations. Therefore if the very illuminator of Luke desired the authority of predecessors for his own faith and preaching, how much more shall I demand for Luke's gospel that authority which was necessary to the gospel of his master?

3. It is another matter if with Marcion the mystery of the Christian religion took its beginning from the discipleship of Luke. But if it ran its course also from of old, it surely had an authentic apparatus, through which it came down even to Luke, by whose attendant testimony Luke too can be admitted. But Marcion, having got hold of Paul's epistle to the Galatians — in which he rebukes even the apostles themselves for not walking with a straight foot toward the truth of the gospel, and at the same time accuses certain false apostles of perverting the gospel of Christ — strives to demolish the standing of those gospels which are published as their own and under the name of the apostles, or even of apostolic men, so that he may, namely, confer upon his own the credit which he takes from them. Now even if Peter and John and James, who were thought to be pillars, were reprehended, the cause is manifest. For with respect to persons they seemed to vary their conduct. And yet, since Paul himself became all things to all men that he might gain all, Peter too may have had this in his counsel, to act somewhat otherwise than he taught. Likewise, if false apostles too had crept in, their character also is published — claiming circumcision and the Jewish calendar. So far were they marked out by Paul not on account of preaching but of conduct — Paul being equally about to mark them out, had they erred in anything concerning God the Creator or his Christ. Therefore the several points will have to be distinguished. If Marcion complains that the apostles are held suspect of prevarication and dissimulation, even to the depraving of the gospel, he now accuses Christ, by accusing those whom Christ chose. But if the apostles did indeed transmit an entire gospel, reprehended only for an inequality of conduct, while the false apostles interpolated their truth, and our writings are derived thence — which then will be that genuine instrument of the apostles, which has suffered adulterers? the one that illumined Paul, and from him Luke? Or, if it has been so utterly destroyed as to have been obliterated, as by a kind of deluge, so by an inundation of falsifiers, then Marcion too has nothing true. Or if that will be the true one, that is, the apostles', which Marcion alone has — then how does that agree with ours which is referred not to the apostles but to Luke? Or if what Marcion uses is not at once to be assigned to Luke because it agrees with ours — adulterated, namely, even as to the title — but is the apostles': then ours too, which agrees with his, is equally the apostles', but adulterated as to the title also.

4. The rope of the contention, then, must be drawn, swaying with equal effort on either side. I call mine true, Marcion his. I affirm Marcion's to be adulterated, Marcion mine. Who shall decide between us, except the reasoning of time — assigning authority to that which shall be found the more ancient, and prejudging vitiation against that which shall later be convicted? For inasmuch as the false is a corruption of the true, by so much must the truth precede the false. A thing will be prior to its undergoing, and the matter prior to its rivalry. Otherwise, how absurd it is, that if we prove ours the more ancient, and Marcion's the later, ours should be thought false before it had its matter from the truth, and Marcion's be believed to have suffered rivalry from ours before it was even published, and finally that should be reckoned the truer which is the later — after so many and so great works and evidences of the Christian religion already published to the world, which surely could not have been published without the truth of the gospel, that is, before the truth of the gospel. As regards, then, the gospel of Luke for the present — inasmuch as its communion between us and Marcion is disputed about the truth — so much more ancient than Marcion is that which is according to us, that Marcion himself once believed in it, when in the first heat of faith he contributed money to the catholic Church, money soon flung out along with himself, after he revolted into his heresy from our truth. What now, if the Marcionites should deny his first faith among us, against his own epistle too? What, if they should not even acknowledge his epistle? Certainly the Antitheses they not only confess to be Marcion's, but even put forward. From these the proof suffices me. For if that gospel which is referred to Luke is among us the very one (let us see whether it be among Marcion too) which Marcion through his Antitheses arraigns as interpolated by the protectors of Judaism toward the embodiment of the law and the prophets — by which they fashioned Christ thence too — surely he could not have arraigned but that which he had found. No one reprehends after the fact things which he is ignorant are to come to be. An emendation does not precede the fault. As an emendator of the gospel overturned from the times of Tiberius even to those of the Antonines, Marcion alone and first turned up, awaited so long by Christ, who now repented that he had hastened to send forth the apostles without the aid of Marcion. Save that heresy is the business of human rashness, not of divine authority, which thus always emends the gospels while it vitiates them — since, even if Marcion is a disciple, he is yet not above his master; and if Marcion is an apostle — "Whether I," says Paul, "or they, so we preach" — and if Marcion is a prophet, "the spirits of the prophets too shall be subject to the prophets: for they are not of subversion, but of peace"; even if Marcion is an angel, he is rather to be called anathema than evangelist, because he evangelized otherwise. And so, while he emends, he confirms both — both ours as the earlier, by emending what he found, and his own as the later, by constituting as new and his own what he established out of the emendation of ours.

5. In sum, if that is the truer which is the prior, that the prior which is also from the beginning, that from the beginning which is from the apostles — it will likewise be established that that has been handed down from the apostles which has been held sacrosanct among the churches of the apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drew from Paul, to what rule the Galatians were brought back, what the Philippians read, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians, what too the Romans of our neighbourhood resound — to whom both Peter and Paul left the gospel sealed even with their own blood. We have the churches that are John's nurslings too. For even though Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, yet the order of bishops, traced back to its origin, will stand upon John as author. So too the high birth of the rest is recognized. I say therefore that among them — and now not only among the apostolic churches, but among all that are confederated with them by the fellowship of the mystery — that gospel of Luke has stood from the beginning of its publication which we most of all defend, whereas Marcion's is to most unknown, and to none known but that it is, by the same fact, condemned. That gospel too has churches, plainly, but its own — as much later as adulterous; whose lineage if you inquire, you will more easily find it apostatic than apostolic, with Marcion, namely, for founder, or some one of Marcion's swarm. Wasps too make combs; Marcionites too make churches. The same authority of the apostolic churches will give patronage to the other gospels too, which we likewise have through them and according to them — John's, I mean, and Matthew's — although that which Mark published is affirmed to be Peter's, whose interpreter Mark was. For Luke's digest too men are wont to ascribe to Paul. It is allowable that what the disciples have promulgated should be regarded as their masters'. And so for these too Marcion is to be pressed — that, omitting them, he rather fastened upon Luke, as though these too had not been among the churches from the beginning, just as Luke also. Nay, it is more credible that these were from the beginning, as prior, since apostolic, since dedicated together with the churches themselves. For the rest, what kind of thing is it, that if the apostles published nothing, the disciples rather published — who could not even have existed as disciples without any teaching of masters? Therefore, since it is established that these too were among the churches, why did Marcion not touch these too — either to be emended, if adulterated, or to be acknowledged, if entire? For it is also fitting that, if any were perverting the gospel, they should rather take care to pervert those whose authority they knew to be the more received. Hence the false apostles too, in that through falsehood they imitated the apostles. Therefore, in so far as he would have emended things which would have had to be emended, if they had been corrupted, by so much he confirmed that those were not corrupted which he thought needed no emendation. In short, he emended what he reckoned corrupted. But neither this with reason, because it was not corrupted. For if the apostolic writings ran their course entire, while Luke's, which is according to us, agrees so with their rule that it abides with them among the churches, then it is established that Luke's too ran its course entire, even to the sacrilege of Marcion. In short, where Marcion laid hands upon it, then it was made diverse from and rival to the apostolic ones. Therefore I will give counsel to his disciples, that either they convert those writings — though late — to the form of his, that they may seem to agree with the apostolic ones (for they do daily reform it, in proportion as they are daily refuted by us), or that they blush for their master, exposed on both sides, since now from conscience he transmits the truth of the gospel, now from shamelessness overturns it. These compendious methods, more or less, we use when we are extricating ourselves against the heretics concerning the faith of the gospel — pleading both the order of times that prescribes against the lateness of falsifiers, and the authority of the churches that gives patronage to the tradition of the apostles, because the truth must precede the false, and must proceed from those by whom it was handed down.

6. But we now enter from here upon another step, summoning, as we have professed, Marcion's gospel itself, intending even so to prove it adulterated. For certainly all that he laboured at — even by building up the Antitheses beforehand — he forces to this end: that he may establish a diversity of the old and new testament, accordingly a Christ of his own separated from the Creator, as of another god, as alien to the law and the prophets. Certainly it was for this that he erased whatever was contrary to his opinion and conspiring with the Creator, as if interwoven by his champions; but whatever was suited to his opinion he reserved. These we will examine, these we will embrace, if they be more for us, if they strike at Marcion's presumption. Then those others too will stand established as erased by the same vice of heretical blindness by which these others were reserved. Thus the intention and form of our little work will hold, under that condition surely which has been agreed upon from either side. Marcion lays it down that there is one Christ who, in the times of Tiberius, was revealed by a hitherto unknown god for the salvation of all nations, another who was destined by the Creator-god for the restitution of the Jewish state, one day to come. Between these he splits a great — nay, a total — difference, as great as between the just and the good, as great as between the law and the gospel, as great as between Judaism and Christianity. Hence will be our objection too, by which we fix it that nothing of the Christ of another god ought to be in common with the Creator; but he is to be pronounced the Creator's if he has administered his arrangements, if he has fulfilled his prophecies, if he has assisted his laws, if he has represented his promises, if he has restored his powers, if he has reformed his opinions, his manners, if he has expressed his properties. Of this compact and this objection, I beg you, reader, be everywhere mindful, and begin to recognize either Marcion's Christ or the Creator's. In the fifteenth year of the principate of Tiberius he sets forth that he came down into the city of Galilee, Capernaum — surely out of the Creator's heaven, into which he had before come down out of his own. Was there, then, any order in this, that he should be described as descending first out of his own heaven into the Creator's? For why should I not reprehend even these things, which do not fulfil the faith of an orderly narrative, ever failing in falsehood? Plainly let these be said once for all, by which we have already elsewhere discussed whether one descending through the Creator, and indeed against the Creator himself, could have been admitted by him, and thence transmitted to an earth equally his own. But now I demand also the rest of the order of the descent, holding that he descended. For let it be his concern, if it is anywhere set down that he appeared. To appear savours of a sudden, unexpected sight — of one who has once dashed his eyes upon that which appeared without delay. But to have descended, while it is being done, is both seen and steals upon the eyes. From the fact itself too it makes an order, and so compels one to ask, in what state, with what bearing, with what onset or tempering, even at what time of day or night, he descended. Moreover, who saw him descending, who reported it, who asseverated a thing surely not to be easily believed even to one asseverating it? It is unworthy, in short, that Romulus should have had a Proculus to affirm his ascent into heaven, but that Christ, a god, should have found no announcer of his descent from his own heaven — as though that other did not ascend by the same ladders of falsehood as this one descended. But what had he to do with Galilee, if he were not the Creator's, to whom that region was destined as he entered upon his preaching? — Isaiah saying, "Drink this first, do it quickly, region of Zabulon and land of Nephthalim, and the rest who are by the sea and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, people who sit in darkness, behold a great light: you who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you." Well, however, that even the god of Marcion is claimed as the illuminator of the nations — by which he ought the rather to have descended even from heaven, and, if at all, to have descended into Pontus rather than into Galilee. For the rest, by both the place and the work of illumination meeting Christ according to the prophecy, we begin already to acknowledge him foretold — showing that at his first entry he came not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfil them. For this Marcion erased as added. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what he straightway did in part. For the prophecy he meanwhile fulfilled as to place. From heaven straight to the synagogue. As the saying goes, "To the matter we have come for, set thy hand, Marcion": take away also that from the gospel, "I am not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and, "It is not to take the bread from the children and give it to the dogs" — namely lest Christ should seem to be Israel's. The deeds suffice me in place of the words. Take away the voices of my Christ — the facts will speak. Behold he comes into the synagogue; certainly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Behold he offers the bread of his teaching first to the Israelites; certainly he prefers them as children. Behold he does not yet impart it to others; certainly he passes them by as dogs. But to whom should he have imparted it more than to the strangers of the Creator, if he had not himself first of all been the Creator's? And yet how could he have been admitted into the synagogue, so sudden, so unknown — of whose tribe, people, house, and lastly of whose registration under Augustus no one was as yet certain, that registration which the Roman archives guard as the most faithful witness of the Lord's nativity? They would surely have remembered, unless they knew him circumcised, that he was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue were entered at large, yet not to teach, save by one well known and tried and approved, long since commended for this very thing, or from elsewhere, with this function. But they were all astonished at his teaching. Plainly. "Because," it says, "his word was in power" — not because he taught against the law and the prophets. For surely the divine utterance furnished both force and grace, building up rather than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise they would not have been astonished, but would have shuddered. Nor would they have marvelled, but would straightway have turned away from a destroyer of the law and the prophets, and surely above all from a preacher of another god — since he could not even have taught against the law and the prophets, and under this title against the Creator, without a profession sent before of a diverse and rival divinity. Since, then, the Scripture signifies nothing of the kind, but only that the force and power of his word were a marvel, it more easily shows that he taught according to the Creator, because it did not deny it, than against the Creator, because it did not signify it. And so either he is to be acknowledged as belonging to him according to whom he taught, or to be judged a prevaricator, if he taught according to him against whom he had come. In the same place the spirit of a demon cries out: "What is there to us and to thee, Jesus? Thou hast come to destroy us. I know who thou art, the Holy One of God." Here I will not discuss whether this surname too suited him whom it would not have been right to call even Christ, were he not the Creator's. Concerning the names the demand has already been made elsewhere. But now I dispute how the demon came to know him called by this name, no preaching ever having been sent forth before concerning him by a god unknown and at that time mute — of whom he could not even attest that he was holy, as one unknown even to his own Creator. But what had he as yet put forth of a new divinity by which he could be understood to be the Holy One of another god? Only that he had entered the synagogue, and had not even by a word done anything against the Creator? As, then, he in no way could have acknowledged as Jesus and the Holy One of God him whom he did not know, so him whom he knew he acknowledged. For he remembered that the prophet had proclaimed the Holy One of God, and that Jesus was the name of God in the son of Nun. These things he had also received from the angel, according to our gospel: "Therefore that which shall be born in thee shall be called holy, the Son of God, and thou shalt call his name Jesus." But he had also surely some sense of the Lord's arrangement (though a demon, yet), rather than of one alien and not yet sufficiently known. For he premised, "What is there to us and to thee?" — not as toward a stranger, this Jesus, to whom the spirits of the Creator pertain. For he did not say, "What is there to thee and to us?" but, "What is there to us and to thee?" — bewailing himself and reproaching himself with his lot; which already seeing he adds, "Thou hast come to destroy us." So far had he acknowledged Jesus to be the Son of a judging and avenging and, so to say, a fierce god, not of that best god who knows neither how to destroy nor to punish. To what end have we premised this passage? That we may teach that Jesus was acknowledged by the demon as none other, and confirmed by himself as none other, than the Creator's. "And yet," you say, "Jesus rebuked him." Plainly, as one invidious, and in his very confession petulant and ill-flattering — as though this were the supreme glory of Christ, if he had come for the destruction of demons and not rather for the salvation of men, who would not have even his disciples glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the white robe of salvation. Or why did he rebuke him? If as one lying altogether, then he was not Jesus, nor the Holy One of God at all; if as one lying in part — in that he had reckoned him indeed Jesus and the Holy One of God, but of the Creator — most unjustly did he rebuke one who thought what he knew ought to be thought, and did not reckon what he was ignorant ought to be reckoned, namely another Jesus and the Holy One of another god. But if the rebuke has no more probable footing than that which we interpret, then the demon too lied in nothing, was not rebuked for a lie; for he himself was Jesus, beside whom the demon could have acknowledged no other, and Jesus confirmed him whom the demon had acknowledged, while he rebukes the demon not for a lie.

8. He was to be called a Nazarene according to the prophecy, the Christ of the Creator. Hence even by that very name we Jews call them Nazarenes after him. For we too are they of whom it is written: "The Nazarites have been made whiter than snow" — they, namely, who formerly were sallow with the stains of delinquency and blackened with the darkness of ignorance. But the appellation of Nazarene was to befit Christ from the hiding-places of his infancy, to which he came down at Nazareth, avoiding Archelaus, son of Herod. This I have not omitted for this reason, that the Christ of Marcion ought to have foresworn all commerce even with the familiar places of the Christ of the Creator — having so many towns of Judea not so emancipated to the Christ of the Creator through the prophets. For the rest, he will be the Christ of the prophets wherever he is found according to the prophets. And yet at Nazareth too nothing new is noted that he preached, while he is reported to have been cast out elsewhere, deservedly on account of a single proverb. Here, observing the hands first laid upon him, I find it necessary now to determine beforehand concerning his bodily substance — that he cannot be believed a phantom who admitted a touch, and that indeed full of violence, being held and seized and dragged even to a precipice. For even though he escaped through their midst, yet he had first experienced force, and was afterward let go — the tumult, namely, being broken up, as is wont, or even burst through, yet not eluded by means of a mist, which would have given way to no touch at all, had it existed. For to touch and to be touched belongs to nothing but a body — even secular wisdom is worthy of the verdict. In short, he himself soon touched others, on whom laying hands (hands surely to be felt), he conferred the benefits of his medicines, as true and as un-imaginary as were the hands through which he conferred them. He, therefore, is the Christ of Isaiah, the remedier of infirmities. "He," it says, "takes away our weaknesses and bears our languors." Now the Greeks are wont to put "to bear" for what is "to take away." Meanwhile the general promise suffices me. Whatever Jesus has cured is mine. We will come, however, to the species of cures too. For the rest, to free from demons too is a cure of infirmity. And so the wicked spirits, as it were from the form of the former example already, went out with testimony, crying out, "Thou art the Son of God." Of what god, let it appear even here. But they were likewise rebuked and bidden to be silent. For accordingly Christ wished to be acknowledged the Son of God by men, not by unclean spirits — that Christ, at least, to whom this befitted, because he had sent before those by whom he could be acknowledged, and surely worthier preachers. To reject the proclamation of an unclean spirit was the part of him who abounded in holy ones. But he who had never been announced — if indeed he wished to be acknowledged, and had come in vain if he did not — would not have spurned the testimony of an alien and any substance whatever, who had none of his own, who had descended into another's. And even now, in so far as he was the destroyer of the Creator, he would have desired nothing more than to be acknowledged and divulged by the very spirits, out of fear; save that Marcion denies that his god is feared, defending that the good is not feared but the judge, with whom are the matters for fear — anger, savagery, judgements, vengeance, condemnation. But the demons too gave way surely out of fear. Therefore they were confessing the Son of a god to be feared — they who would have had occasion not to give way, had they not had to fear. And he, expelling them by command and rebuke, not by persuasion (as the good), showed himself one to be feared. Or did he perhaps rebuke them for this reason, that he was feared, being unwilling to be feared? And how did he wish them to go out, which they would not do but out of fear? He fell, then, into a necessity by which he behaved unlike his own nature, when he could, as the good, have spared them once for all. He fell also into another mark of prevarication, when he allowed himself to be feared by the demons as the Son of the Creator — so that now not by his own power did he expel the demons, but through the authority of the Creator. He goes forth into the wilderness. Solemn, and of this kind, is the region of the Creator. It behoved the Word to be seen there too in body, where he had once acted even in cloud. The state of the place too suited the gospel, which had pleased the law. Let the wilderness, then, take up joyfulness — this Isaiah had promised. Detained by the crowds, "It behoves me," he says, "to announce the kingdom of God to other cities also." Had he already anywhere shown his god? I think not yet. But was he speaking to those who knew another god too? Neither do I believe this. Therefore, if neither he had published another god nor they knew any besides the Creator, he was portending the kingdom of the same god whom alone he knew to be known to those who heard.

9. Out of so many kinds of works, why did he look especially to fishing, that from it he should take into the apostolate Simon and the sons of Zebedee (for it cannot seem a simple deed, from which an argument was to proceed), saying to Peter, trembling at the copious haul of fish, "Fear not, for henceforth thou shalt be catching men"? For by this saying he was suggesting to them an understanding of the prophecy fulfilled — that he was the one who had pronounced through Jeremiah, "Behold, I will send many fishers, and they shall fish them," men namely. In short, leaving their little boats they followed him, understanding him to be the very one who had begun to do what he had foretold. It is another matter if he affected to choose out of the guild of boatmen, intending one day to have for his apostle the skipper Marcion. We have indeed shown beforehand, against the Antitheses, that nothing avails to Marcion's design what he thinks a diversity of law and gospel — since this too was arranged by the Creator, and in short foretold in the promise of a new law and a new word and a new testament. But since he argues rather attentively, with that I-know-not-what fellow-sufferer of his and co-hateful one, concerning the cleansing of the leper, it will not irk me to meet him and first to show the force of the figurative law, which in the example of the leper not to be touched — nay, to be removed from all commerce — forbade communion with a man stained by sins; with such as these the apostle too forbids even to take food; for the brands of sins are shared, as by contagion, if anyone has mingled himself with a sinner. And so the Lord, wishing the law to be understood more deeply as signifying spiritual things through carnal — and on this account not destroying but rather building up — wishing to be acknowledged in a more pertinent sense, touched the leper, by whom even if a man could have been defiled, God surely would not be defiled, being incontaminable. Thus it will not be objected to him that he ought to have observed the law and not touched the unclean, whom the touch of the unclean was not going to defile. That this rather suits my Christ I teach thus, while I demonstrate that it does not suit yours. For if as the rival of the law he touched the leper, making nothing of the precept of the law through contempt of defilement, how could he be defiled who had no body to be defiled? For a phantom could not be defiled. He therefore who could not be defiled, as a phantom, will now be incontaminable not by divine power, but by the emptiness of a phantom; nor can he seem to have despised defilement, of which he had no matter; nor so to have destroyed the law, who had escaped defilement from the occasion of being a phantom, not from the display of power. But if Elisha, the prophet of the Creator, cleansed the single leper Naaman the Syrian out of so many Israelite lepers, neither does this make for a diversity of Christ, as though in this way the better — in that a stranger cleanses an Israelite leper whom his own lord could not cleanse — the Syrian the more easily cleansed signifying, through the nations, of those who bristled with the seven stains of capital delinquencies — idolatry, blasphemy, homicide, adultery, fornication, false testimony, fraud — the cleansing in Christ, the light of those nations. Wherefore seven times, as though through each several head, he washed in the Jordan — at once that he might sing the expiation of the whole week, and because the force and fullness of a single washing was consecrated to Christ alone, who was to make on earth, as a shortened word, so a shortened washing. For this too Marcion objects, that Elisha needed matter, employed water, and that seven times, whereas Christ, by a word alone, and that once, performed and represented the cure forthwith. As though I should not dare to claim the very word too for the substance of the Creator. Of no thing is he not the more powerful author who is the prior. It is plainly incredible that the power of the Creator should have wrought by a word the remedy of a single defect, who by a word brought forth at once so great a mass of the world. Whence is the Christ of the Creator the more discerned than from the power of his word? But for this reason another Christ, because otherwise than Elisha, because more powerful than his own servant! What do you establish, Marcion — that things are done in the same way by servants as by the very masters? Are you not afraid lest it turn to your disgrace, if you deny Christ to be the Creator's because he was more powerful than the Creator's servant — who is acknowledged greater compared to the littleness of Elisha, if indeed greater? For the cure is equal, though the operation differ. What more did your Christ furnish than my Elisha? Nay, what great thing did the word of your Christ furnish, when it furnished what the river of the Creator did? According to these, the rest too occur. For inasmuch as it pertained to the aversion of human glory, he forbade him to divulge it; but inasmuch as it pertained to the safeguarding of the law, he bade the order be fulfilled. "Go, show thyself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded." For the figurative arguments, as of the prophesied law, he still protected in their own images — which signified that a man once a sinner, presently cleansed by the word of God, ought to offer a gift to God at the temple, namely prayer and thanksgiving at the church through Christ Jesus, the catholic priest of the Father. And so he added, "That it may be to you for a testimony" — without doubt that by which he testified that he did not dissolve the law but fulfil it; by which he testified that he himself was the one announced as about to take up their diseases and infirmities. This so congruent and due interpretation of the testimony, the flatterer of his own Christ, Marcion, under pretext of mildness and gentleness, seeks to exclude. For "as good too," he says, "knowing besides that everyone freed from leprosy would carry out the solemnities of the law, for that reason he so commanded." What then? Did he persevere in goodness, that is, in the permission of the law, or not? For if he persevered as good, he will never be the destroyer of the law, nor be held to be of another god, the destruction of the law ceasing through which he is claimed for another god. If he did not persevere as good, by destroying the law afterward, then he placed a false testimony afterward among them in the cure of the leper; for he deserted goodness while he destroys the law. He is now evil, when overturner of the law, if good, when indulger of the law. But also, in that he indulged obedience to the law, he confirmed the law to be good. For no one suffers obedience to be paid to an evil thing. Therefore even so he is evil, if he indulged obedience to an evil law, and so worse, if he came as the destroyer of a good law. Accordingly, if he commanded the gift to be offered because he knew everyone freed from leprosy would so do, he could also not have commanded what he knew would be done spontaneously. In vain, then, did he come down, as though to destroy the law, when he yields to the obeyers of the law. And yet, as knowing their disposition, he ought rather to have anticipated, to avert them the more from it, if for this he had come. Why, then, did he not keep silent, that a man should obey the law by his own choice alone? — for then at least he might somewhat seem to have stood by his patience. But he even adds his own authority, magnified by the weight of testimony. Of what testimony now, except of the law asserted? Certainly it makes no difference in what way he confirmed the law — whether as good, or as superfluous, or as patient, or as inconstant — provided I drive you, Marcion, from your footing. Behold, he commanded the law to be fulfilled. In whatever way he commanded, in the same he could also have premised that opinion, "I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil." What, then, was it to you to have erased from the gospel what is safe? For you confessed that he did out of goodness what you deny he said. It is established, then, that he said it, because he also did it, and that you rather have erased the Lord's voice from the gospel than that our people have inserted it.

10. The paralytic too is cured, and that in a gathering, the people looking on. "For the people," says Isaiah, "shall see the loftiness of the Lord and the glory of God." What loftiness, and what glory? "Be strong, you hands let down, and you knees dissolved" — this will be the paralysis. "Be strong, and fear not." Not idly repeating "Be strong," nor in vain subjoining "Fear not," since with the reintegration of the limbs he was also promising a representation of strength: "Arise, and take up thy bed" — at once a vigour of mind too, toward not fearing those who were to say, "Who shall forgive sins but God alone?" You have, then, already both the discharged prophecy of a special medicine, and of the things which followed the medicine. Likewise recognize Christ the remitter of delinquencies in the same prophet. "For," it says, "in many he shall remit their delinquencies, and our delinquencies he himself takes away." For also in the former passage, from the person of the Lord himself: "Though your delinquencies be as scarlet, I will whiten them as snow; though as crimson, I will whiten them as wool" — in the scarlet showing the blood of the prophets, in the crimson that of the Lord, as the brighter. Micah too concerning the pardon of delinquencies: "What god is like thee, taking away iniquities and passing over injustices to the remnant of thine inheritance? And he held not his anger for a testimony, because he willed to be merciful; he will turn, and have mercy upon us; he will sink our delinquencies, and he will sink our sins into the depth of the sea." But even if nothing of the kind had been foretold concerning Christ, I should have examples of this benignity in the Creator, promising me the Father's affections in the Son too. I see the Ninevites obtain pardon of their crimes from the Creator — not to say, then too from Christ, because from the beginning he acted in the Father's name. I read too that Nathan the prophet said to David, acknowledging his delinquency in the matter of Uriah, "And the Lord has put away thy delinquency, and thou shalt not die"; likewise that king Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, guilty of idolatry and of the blood of Naboth, earned pardon under the name of penitence; that Jonathan, son of Saul, by entreaty blotted out the fault of an unsealed fast. Why should I weave again about the people itself, so often restored by indulgence of delinquencies? — by that god, namely, who prefers mercy to sacrifice, and the penitence of the sinner to his death. It is prior, then, that you deny that the Creator ever indulged delinquencies; the consequence is that you show that he foretold no such thing concerning his Christ either; and so you will prove this new benignity of the new Christ, if you have proved it neither equal to the Creator's nor foretold by the Creator. But whether to remit sins can belong to him who is denied to retain them, and whether it belongs to him to absolve whose it is not also to condemn, and whether it suits one to forgive against whom nothing has been committed — having engaged elsewhere already, we preferred to admonish rather than to discuss. Concerning "Son of man" our objection is twofold: that Christ could not lie, so as to pronounce himself Son of man if he were not truly so; nor be constituted Son of man who was not born of a man, either father or mother; and so it must be discussed of what man he ought to be taken as son, of father or of mother. If he is of God the Father, surely he is not of man; if not also of man, it remains that he is of a man for mother; if of a man, it now appears that he is of a virgin. For to whom a man is not given as father, neither will a husband be reckoned to his mother; and to whose mother a husband is not reckoned, she is a virgin. For the rest, two fathers will now be reckoned, God and man, if the mother be not a virgin. For she will have a husband, so as not to be a virgin, and by having a husband she will make two fathers, God and man, for him who should be the son both of God and of man. Such a nativity, if at all, the fables ascribe to Castor or Hercules. If these things are thus distinguished — that is, if he is the son of man from his mother because he is not from a father, but from a virgin mother because not from a human father — this will be the Christ of Isaiah, whom he proclaims a virgin should conceive. By what reasoning, then, you can admit "Son of man," Marcion, I cannot see all around. If of a human father, you deny him the Son of God; if of God too, you make Christ a Hercules out of the fable; if only of a human mother, you grant me mine; if neither of a human father, then he is the son of no man, and of necessity he must have admitted a lie, who said himself to be what he was not. One thing can come to the aid of your straits: if you dare either to surname even your god, the Father of Christ, a man too — which Valentinus did of his Aeon — or to deny the virgin a human being, which not even Valentinus did. What now, if by the very title of Son of man Christ is reckoned in Daniel? Does it not suffice for proof of the prophetic Christ? For when he calls himself that which was proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator, without doubt he offers himself to be understood as the very one concerning whom it was proclaimed. A community of names may, if at all, seem simple — and yet we maintain that he ought to be called neither Christ nor Jesus, holding the condition of diversity. But the appellation which is "Son of man," in so far as it comes by accident, by so much is it difficult that it too should concur over and above the community of name. For it is from a proper accident — especially since the same cause does not agree by which it comes into community. And indeed if Marcion's Christ too were said to be born of a man, then he too would take up a community of appellation, and there would be two sons of man, just as also two Christs and two Jesuses. Therefore, since the appellation is proper to him in whom it has its cause, if it be claimed also for another in whom there is a community of the name, not also of the appellation — the community of name too now becomes suspect in him for whom a community of appellation is claimed without a cause; and it follows that he is believed one and the same who is found more capable both of the name and of the appellation, while the other is excluded who has no community of appellation, lacking the cause. Nor will another be more capable of both than he who is prior, and both obtained the name of Christ and the appellation of Son of man — Jesus, namely, the Creator's. This was the one seen by the Babylonian king in the furnace with his martyrs, the fourth, as the Son of man. The same was revealed directly to Daniel himself, the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, a judge, as the Scripture also demonstrates. This I have said could have sufficed concerning the prophetic naming touching the Son of man. But the Scripture confers more upon me — by the interpretation, namely, of the Lord himself. For when the Jews, looking only at his manhood, and not yet certain of his Godhead, in that he was the Son of God too, rightly debated that a man could not remit delinquencies, but God alone — why did he not, according to their intention, answer them of a man, that he had power to remit delinquencies, since by naming Son of man he would name a man? — unless because by the very appellation of Son of man, from the instrument of Daniel, he willed to strike them back, that he might show a God and a man who remits delinquencies; namely that sole Son of man in the prophecy of Daniel, who obtained the power of judging, and through it surely of remitting delinquencies too (for he who judges, also absolves) — so that, this scandal being discussed through the recollection of Scripture, they might the more easily acknowledge him to be the very Son of man from the very remission of sins. In short, nowhere yet had he professed himself the Son of man before that passage, the first in which he first remitted sins, that is, in which he first judged, while he absolved. To these, whatever the opposite party shall have argued, consider what it is. For of necessity it tends to that madness, that it both defends the Son of man, lest it make him a liar, and denies that he was born of man, lest it grant the Son of a virgin. But if both divine authority and the nature of things and common wisdom do not admit the heretical insanity, there is occasion here too of interposing most briefly concerning the substance of the body, against the phantoms of Marcion. If he is born of a man, as Son of man, his body is from a body. Plainly you may more easily find a man born without a heart or brain, like Marcion himself, than without a body, like Marcion's Christ. And so look into the heart, or brain, of the man of Pontus.

11. He brings forward into argument the publican chosen by the Lord, as though chosen by an adversary of the law, a stranger to the law and profane to Judaism. It escaped him even concerning Peter, a man of the law, and yet not only chosen but having attained the testimony of an acknowledgement bestowed by the Father. Nowhere had he read that Christ was proclaimed the light and hope and expectation of the nations. And yet he rather approved the Jews by saying that a physician is not necessary for the sound, but for the sick. For if he wished the ethnics and publicans, whom he chose, to be understood as the sick, he was confirming the Jews to be sound, for whom he denied a physician necessary. If this is so, ill did he come down to destroy the law, as if to remedy bad health, in which those who walked were in good health, for whom a physician was not necessary. But what kind of thing is it that he should set forth the likeness of a physician and not fulfil it? For just as no one applies a physician to the sound, so neither to men so estranged as a man is from the god of Marcion, having both his author and his protector, and from him rather Christ for a physician. The likeness prejudges this — that a physician is rather furnished by him to whom belong those who languish. But whence did John too come into the midst? Suddenly Christ, suddenly John too. Such are all things with Marcion, which have their own and full order with the Creator. But of John the rest elsewhere. For we must answer each several joint as it presents itself. Now I will maintain this, to demonstrate that both John suits Christ and Christ John — both surely the prophet of the Creator, since the Christ of the Creator — and so let the heretic blush, having frustrated in vain the order of John. For if John had administered nothing at all — the crier, according to Isaiah, in the wilderness and the preparer of the Lord's ways through the denunciation and the laudation of penitence — if he had not also dipped him among the rest, no one would have provoked the disciples of Christ, eating and drinking, to the form of the disciples of John, assiduously fasting and praying; because, if any diversity stood between Christ and John and the flock of each, there would be no force in the comparison, the intention of the challenge would be void. For no one would marvel and no one would be tormented, if the preachings of a diverse and rival divinity did not agree with one another in their disciplines too, not first agreeing about the authorities of their disciplines. So far was Christ John's and John Christ's — both the Creator's, and both of the law and the prophets, preachers and masters. But Christ would also have rejected John's discipline, as of another god, and would have defended the disciples, as rightly walking otherwise — initiated, namely, into another and contrary divinity. But as it is, humbly rendering the reason that the sons of the bridegroom could not fast so long as the bridegroom was with them, but afterward promising that they would fast when the bridegroom should be taken from them, he neither defended the disciples but rather excused them, as reprehended not without reason, nor rejected John's discipline, but rather conceded it — assigning it to John's time, as destining it for his own time — though he would otherwise have rejected it and defended its rivals, had not what already was not already been his own. I hold my Christ even in the name of bridegroom, concerning whom the psalm: "He, like a bridegroom going forth from his chamber: from the height of heaven his going forth, and his return to the very height of it." Who also, through Isaiah, rejoicing toward the Father, says, "Let my soul exult in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation, and with the tunic of joyfulness as a bridegroom; he has set a mitre about me as about a bride." For in himself he reckons the Church too, concerning which the same spirit to him: "And thou shalt set them all about thee as the ornament of a bride." This bride Christ fetches for himself, even through Solomon, from the calling of the nations. Indeed you have read, "Come, bride, from Lebanon" — the mention of mount Lebanon being elegantly thrown in, which by the word for frankincense is among the Greeks; for out of idolatry he was espousing the Church to himself. Deny now that you are most insane, Marcion. Behold, you assail the law of your own god too. He does not join marriages, the joined he does not admit; he dips no one but the celibate or the eunuch; he reserves baptism for death or for divorce. Why, then, do you make his Christ a bridegroom? This is the name of him who joined male and female, not of him who separated. You have erred also in that pronouncement of the Lord by which he seems to discern new and old. You have been puffed up with the old skins and made brainless with the new wine, and so to the old, that is, the former gospel, you have sewed a patch of heretical novelty. In which point another Creator — I would learn — when through Jeremiah he commanded, "Make for yourselves a new freshness," did he not turn them away from the old? When through Isaiah he declares, "The old things have passed, and behold the new which I make," did he not convert them to the new? Long ago we laid it down that this destination of the former things, promised rather by the Creator, is exhibited by Christ, under the authority of one and the same god, whose are both the old and the new. For neither does he commit new wine into old skins who has not also had old skins, and no one puts a new addition upon an old garment but he to whom an old garment too is not wanting. He does not do a thing, if it is not to be done, who has whence to do it, if it were to be done. And so if in this he was directing the likeness, to show that he separated the novelty of the gospel from the oldness of the law, he was demonstrating that even that which he separated was his own, and was not to be marked off by the separation of things alien — because no one adds his own things to alien, that he may be able to separate them from the alien. Separation takes place through a conjunction from which it is made. Thus the things which he separated he also showed to have been in one, just as they would have been, had he not separated. And yet even so we grant this separation through reformation, through amplitude, through advance — just as fruit is separated from the seed, when it is yet fruit from the seed: so the gospel too is separated from the law, while it is brought forward out of the law, other than it, but not alien — diverse, but not contrary. Nor is the form of speech in Christ new. When he sets forth likenesses, when he refutes questions, it comes from the seventy-seventh psalm: "I will open," it says, "my mouth in a parable" — that is, a likeness; "I will utter problems" — that is, I will expound questions. If you had wished to prove him a man of another nation, surely you would prove it from a property of speech.

12. Concerning the sabbath too I premise this, that this question could not have arisen if Christ did not carry about the Lord of the sabbath. For it would not be debated why he destroyed the sabbath, if he ought to destroy it. Now he ought to destroy it, if he were of another god, and no one would marvel at him doing what befitted that other. They marvelled, then, because it did not befit him to carry about the Creator-god and to assail his sabbath. And, that we may settle each first point — lest we everywhere renew the same against every argumentation of the adversary that rests on some new institution of Christ — this definition shall now stand: that there was debate about the novelty of any institution because about the novelty of divinity nothing had as yet been published, just as neither debated; nor can it be retorted from the very novelty of any institution that another divinity than the Creator's was sufficiently demonstrated by Christ, since the very novelty too, foretold by the Creator, has been established not to be marvelled at in Christ. And surely another god ought first to have been set forth, afterward his discipline brought in — because a god furnishes authority to a discipline, not a discipline to a god; unless indeed Marcion plainly did not learn letters so perverse through a master, but a master through letters. The rest concerning the sabbath I direct thus. If Christ broke into the sabbath, he did it according to the example of the Creator — seeing that, in the siege of the city of Jericho, the ark of the testament being carried about the walls for eight days, even on the sabbath, by the precept of the Creator, the sabbath was destroyed by working, as those think who reckon this even of Christ, being ignorant that neither Christ destroyed the sabbath nor the Creator, as we shall presently teach. And yet through Joshua then too the sabbath was shaken, that this also might be reported of Christ; even if he pursued with hatred the most solemn day of the Jews — that Christ, not of the Jews, professing the Creator even by his hatred of the sabbath, as the Christ of him, was following him who cries out by the mouth of Isaiah, "Your new moons and your sabbaths my soul hates." But however these things may be said, we know that even in this species an abrupt defence must be applied against an abrupt provocation. Now I will dispute even to the very matter, in which the discipline of Christ seemed to destroy the sabbath. The disciples had hungered; on that day they had rubbed out ears plucked with their hands; having worked a food, they had broken the holy-days. Christ excuses them, and is liable for the sabbath violated; the Pharisees accuse him; Marcion catches at the state of the controversy (that I may play a little with the truth of my Lord) of the letter and of the will. For from the Scripture of the Creator there is taken — and from the will of Christ a colour, as from the example of David entering the temple on the sabbath and boldly working a food, the loaves of proposition being broken. For he too remembered that this privilege had been granted to the sabbath from the beginning, from which the day itself was discovered — pardon of fasting, I mean. For when the Creator had forbidden the manna to be gathered for two days, he permitted it only on the preparation-day, that the previous provision of food might free the holy-days of the following sabbath from fasting. Well, then, that the Lord too followed the same cause in the destruction (if they wish it so called) of the sabbath; well that he expressed the affection of the Creator too in the honour of not fasting on the sabbath. In short, then at last would he have destroyed the sabbath — and the Creator himself — if he had commanded the disciples to fast on the sabbath against the standing of the letter and will of the Creator. But since he did not constantly protect the disciples, but excuses them; since he opposes human necessity as a kind of intercessor; since he keeps a preferable honour of the sabbath, of not saddening rather than of being idle; since he equates David and his companions with his own disciples in fault and in pardon; since it pleases him that the Creator indulged; since out of his example he too is so good — is he therefore alien to the Creator? Thereupon the Pharisees observed whether he would work cures on the sabbath, that they might accuse him — certainly as the destroyer of the sabbath, not as the professor of a new god; for perhaps I shall everywhere drive in this one point, that another Christ was nowhere proclaimed. But the Pharisees erred altogether about the law of the sabbath, not noticing that it indicated conditionally the holy-days of works, under a certain species of them. For when he says of the sabbath day, "Thou shalt not do in it any work of thine," by saying "thine" he defined it of human work, which each performs from his craft or business, not of the divine. But the work of salvation and of soundness is not man's but God's own. Just as again in the law, "Thou shalt not," it says, "do any work in it, except what shall be done for every soul" — that is, in the cause of freeing a soul: because the work of God can be done even through a man unto the salvation of a soul, yet from God; which Christ too, a man, was to do, because also God. Into this sense of the law, then, wishing to bring them through the restoration of the withered hand, he asks, "Is it lawful on the sabbaths to do well, or not? to free a soul, or to destroy it?" — that by permitting that work which he was to do for a soul, he might admonish them what works of the sabbath the law forbade, namely human, and what it enjoined, namely divine, which should be done for every soul. He is called Lord of the sabbath, because he protected the sabbath as his own thing. And even if he had destroyed it, with reason, as Lord — rather he who instituted it. But he did not destroy it at all, as Lord — so that from this it may now appear that not even then, in the carrying about of the ark at Jericho, was the sabbath destroyed by the Creator. For that too was a work of God which he himself had commanded, and which he had arranged for the souls of his own men set in the crisis of war. But even if he somewhere professed hatred of the sabbaths — by saying "Your sabbaths," reckoning them men's, not his, which a people full of delinquencies celebrates without fear of God, loving God with the lips, not the heart — for their sabbaths, that is, whatever was done by his discipline, he made another state, which through the same prophet he afterward pronounces true and dainty and not to be profaned. Thus neither does Christ rescind the sabbath at all, whose law he held both above in the cause of the disciples, working for a soul (for he indulged the comfort of food to the hungry), and now in curing the withered hand — everywhere driving in by his deeds, "I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil," if Marcion with this voice has stopped his mouth. For here too he fulfilled the law, while he interprets its condition, illumines the difference of works, while he does what the law excepts concerning the holy-days of the sabbath, while he makes the very sabbath day, holy from the beginning by the Father's blessing, holier by his own benefaction — on which, namely, he ministered divine helps, which an adversary would have furnished on other days, that he might not adorn the sabbath of the Creator, that he might not render to the sabbath its due works. On which day, if Elisha the prophet too restored to life the dead son of the Shunammite, you see, Pharisee, and you, Marcion, that it was of old the Creator's to do well on the sabbaths, to free a soul, not to destroy it — that Christ brought in nothing new which is not of the form, the gentleness, the mercy, the proclamation too of the Creator. For here too he represents the prophecy of a special medicine. The dissolved hands grow strong, just as the dissolved knees in the paralytic.

13. Certainly he evangelizes to Zion and Jerusalem peace and all good things; certainly he ascends into the mountain and there passes the night in prayer, and surely is heard by the Father. Unroll, then, the prophets, and recognize the whole order. "Ascend into a high mountain," says Isaiah, "thou who evangelizest Zion; lift up thy voice with vigour, thou who evangelizest Jerusalem." Still in vigour they were astounded at his teaching; for he was teaching as one having power. And again: "Therefore the people shall know my name in that day." What name, but Christ's? "Because I am the very one who speaks." For then he himself it was who spoke in the prophets — the Word, the Son of the Creator. "I am present, while it is the hour, in the mountains, as one evangelizing the hearing of peace, as one evangelizing good things." Likewise Nahum of the twelve: "For behold, swift feet upon the mountain of one evangelizing peace." But of the voice of nocturnal prayer to the Father, manifestly the psalm: "My God, I will cry by day, and thou wilt hear, and by night, and not unto vanity for me." And elsewhere, of the same place and voice, the psalm: "With my voice I cried out to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain." You have the representation of the name, you have the act of one evangelizing, you have the place of the mountain, and the time of night, and the sound of the voice, and the hearing of the Father; you have the Christ of the prophets. But why did he choose twelve apostles, and not some other number? Nay, from this too I could interpret my Christ, foretold not only by the voices of the prophets, but by the arguments of facts. For I detect figures of this number with the Creator: the twelve springs of Elim, and the twelve gems in the priestly tunic of Aaron, and the twelve stones chosen by Joshua out of the Jordan and laid up in the ark of the testament. For just so many apostles were portended — to water, like springs and rivers, the orb of the nations once arid and deserted of knowledge (as also through Isaiah: "I will set rivers in a waterless land"); like gems, to illumine the sacred vestment of the Church, which Christ the priest of the Father has put on; like stones too, solid in faith, whom the true Joshua chose out of the washing of the Jordan and received into the sanctuary of his testament. What of the kind suits Marcion's Christ, as concerns the defence of the number? A thing cannot seem done simply by him which can be seen not done simply by mine. The thing will belong to him with whom the preparation of the thing is found. He changes Peter's name too from Simon — because the Creator too reformed the names of Abraham and Sarah and Hoshea, calling this one Jesus, to those adding syllables. But why Peter? If on account of vigour of faith, many materials of solidity would have lent their name from their own. Or because Christ too is both a rock and a stone? Seeing that we also read him set as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence. I pass over the rest. And so he affected to communicate to his dearest disciple a name peculiarly from his own figures — I think more nearly than from things not his own. There meet him from Tyre and from other regions a multitude, even from beyond the sea. To this the psalm looked: "And behold, foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians, these were there. 'Mother Zion,' a man shall say, and a man was made in her" (since God was born a man), "and he built her by the will of the Father" — that you may know that the Gentiles then came together to him, because God was born a man, about to build the Church by the will of the Father, out of foreigners too. So too Isaiah: "Behold, these come from afar, and these from the north and the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." Concerning whom again: "Lift up thine eyes round about, and see, all are gathered together." Concerning whom too below: "Thou seest the unknown and the strangers, and thou shalt say to thy heart, Who has begotten these to me? and who has reared these for me? but where were these for me?" This will be the Christ not of the prophets? And who will be the Christ of the Marcionites? If perversity pleases — he who was not the prophets'.

14. I come now to his ordinary opinions, through which he introduces the property of his teaching unto an edict, so to say, of Christ: "Blessed are the beggars" (for so the interpretation of the word that is in Greek requires) "for theirs is the kingdom of God." Now this very thing, that he began from benedictions, is the Creator's, who dedicated the universe, as he produced it, by no other voice than that of benediction. "For my heart," he says, "has belched forth an excellent word." This will be the excellent word, of benediction namely, which is acknowledged also as the initiator of the new testament from the old example. What wonder, then, if he entered also upon the affections of the Creator — through utterance of this kind ever loving the beggars and poor and lowly and widows and orphans, consoling, asserting, avenging them? — so that you may believe this as it were private benignity of Christ a rivulet from the fountains of the Saviour. In truth, where to direct myself I know not, in so great a frequency of utterances of this kind, as in a wood or in a meadow or in an orchard of apples. The thing must be sought at random, as it falls. The psalm cries out: "Judge the orphan and the beggar, and deal justly with the lowly and the poor; free the poor, and rescue the beggar from the hand of the sinner." Likewise the seventy-first psalm: "Justice shall judge the beggars of the people, and shall make safe the sons of the poor." And in what follows, concerning Christ: "All nations shall serve him." But David ruled over the one Jewish nation — lest anyone think it said of David, because he too had taken up the lowly and those labouring under necessities. "Because," it says, "he shall free the beggar from the strong, he shall spare the beggar and the poor, and the souls of the poor he shall make safe; from usury and injustice he shall redeem their souls, and honoured shall be their name in his sight." Likewise: "Let sinners be turned into the underworld, all the nations that forget God; because the beggar shall not be held in forgetfulness unto the end, the endurance of the poor shall not perish unto the end." Likewise: "Who is like our God, who dwells on high, and beholds lowly things in heaven and on earth, who raises up the beggar from the earth, and exalts the poor from the dung-heap, that he may make him sit with the princes of the people" — surely in his kingdom. So too of old in Kingdoms, Hannah, the mother of Samuel, rendering glory to God in spirit, "Who," she says, "raises the poor from the earth and the beggar, that he may make him sit with the chiefs of the people" — surely in his kingdom — "and on thrones of glory" — surely royal ones. But through Isaiah, how he inveighs against the harassers of the needy: "But you, to what end do you set fire to my vineyard, and the spoil of the beggar in your houses? Why do you injure my people, and confound the face of the beggars?" And again: "Woe to those who write wickedness, for in writing they write wickedness, avoiding the judgements of the beggars and seizing the things judged for the poor of my people." Which judgements he demands for orphans and widows too, as for the needy of comfort. "Judge the orphan, and deal justly with the widow, and come, let us be reconciled, says the Lord." Whose so great affection toward every condition of lowliness is the Creator's, his too will be the kingdom which is promised by Christ, to whose affection those have long since belonged to whom it is promised. For even if you think the Creator's promises were earthly, but Christ's heavenly — well that heaven appears, as yet, of no other god than him whose the earth too is; well that the Creator promised at least the lesser things, that I may the more easily believe him about the greater too, than him who never first built up the faith of his liberality concerning the lesser. "Blessed are they that hunger, for they shall be filled." I might have transmitted this title to the former, since the hungry are none other than the poor and beggars, were it not that the Creator had destined this promise too specially toward the prebuilding, namely, of his own gospel — seeing that through Isaiah, concerning those whom he was to call from the height of the earth, surely the nations: "Behold," he says, "swiftly, lightly they shall come" — swiftly, as hastening under the ends of the times; lightly, because without the burdens of the former law. "They shall not hunger, nor thirst." Therefore they shall be filled — which surely is not promised but to the hungry and thirsty. And again: "Behold," he says, "those who serve me shall be filled, but you shall hunger: behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst." We shall see these contraries too, whether they are pre-ministered to Christ. Meanwhile, that he promises fullness to the hungry is the Creator-god's. "Blessed are they that weep, for they shall laugh." Run through the opinion of Isaiah: "Behold, those who serve me shall exult in joyfulness, but you shall be confounded: behold, those who serve me shall be delighted, but you shall cry out for sorrow of heart." Recognize these contraries too with Christ. Certainly delight and exultation in joyfulness are promised to those who are in the diverse condition, the sad and gloomy and anxious. And the psalm too, the 125th: "Those who sow," it says, "in tears, shall reap in exultation." Now to those exulting and taking joyfulness laughter accrues, as to the mourning and grieving weeping. Thus the Creator, proclaiming the matters of laughter and of weeping, said first that the weeping shall laugh. Therefore he who began from the consolation of the poor and lowly and hungry and weeping, straightway desired to represent that one whom he had demonstrated through Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to evangelize to the poor" — "Blessed are the beggars, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven"; "he has sent me to heal the broken in heart" — "Blessed are they that hunger, for they shall be filled"; "to call the languishing" — "Blessed are they that weep, for they shall laugh"; "to give to the mourners of Zion glory, and for ashes the joyfulness of ointment, and the garment of glory for the spirit of weariness." If Christ, admitted at once, administered these things, either he himself is the one who proclaimed that he would come to these things, or, if he has not yet come who proclaimed, ridiculously, but of necessity I might perhaps say, he commanded the Christ of Marcion: "Blessed shall you be, when men shall hold you in hatred, and shall reproach you, and shall cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man's sake." By this pronouncement, without doubt, he exhorts to endurance. What less does the Creator through Isaiah? "Fear not the ignominy from men, and by their nullification be not diminished." What ignominy, what nullification? That which was to be for the Son of man's sake. Who is this? He who is according to the Creator. Whence shall we prove it? By the destruction proclaimed against him too; as through Isaiah, to the Jews, the authors of the hatred: "Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations"; and elsewhere: "Sanctify him who circumscribes his own soul, who is held in spurning by the nations, by their servants and magistrates." For if the hatred was proclaimed against that Son of man who is according to the Creator, and the gospel attests that the name of Christians, surely derived from Christ, shall be hated for the Son of man's sake, which is Christ — then he constitutes as the cause of the hatred that Son of man who was according to the Creator, against whom the hatred was proclaimed. And surely if he had not yet come, the hatred of the name, which is carried on today, could not have preceded the person of the name.
