For both there is sanctifying among us, and one circumscribes his own soul, laying it down for us, and is held in spurning by the nations. And he who is born, he will be the Son of man, for whom our name too is refused.

15. "After these things," it says, "did their fathers to the prophets." O versatile Christ — now the destroyer, now the asserter of the prophets! He destroyed as their rival, converting their disciples; he asserted them for himself as a friend, censuring their persecutors. Now in so far as the asserting of the prophets, to whose destruction he had come, would not suit the Christ of Marcion, by so much the censuring of the persecutors of the prophets, whom he fulfilled in all things, suits the Christ of the Creator — or because it is rather the Creator's to reproach the fathers' delinquencies to their sons than that god's who castigates not even each one's own. "But not at once," you say, "did he protect the prophets, if he wished the iniquity of the Jews to be affirmed, that they had not even dealt piously with their prophets." And yet no iniquity here was to be reproached to the Jews — rather they were to be praised and approved, if they censured those to whose destruction, after so great an age, the best god was moved. But, I think, now no longer best, now somewhat lingering even with the Creator, nor altogether the god of Epicurus. For behold he changes into a malediction, and shows himself one who knows how to be offended and to grow angry. For he says "Woe." But a question arises for us concerning the quality of that word, as though it were not so much of malediction as of admonition. And what is the difference, when even an admonition is not made without the sting of a threat, made especially the more bitter through the "Woe"? Both an admonition and a threat too will belong to him who knows how to be angry. For no one admonishes and no one threatens, that one may not do something, but he who will avenge it when done. No one would avenge but he who knows how to be angry. Others indeed acknowledge a word of malediction, but they would have Christ pronounce "Woe" thus, not as it were properly from his own opinion, but because the "Woe" is from the Creator, and that he wished to oppose to them the harshness of the Creator, that he might commend his own forbearance above in the benedictions. As though it did not befit the Creator, as furnishing both — both a good god and a judge — to subjoin in maledictions also severity, since he had premised benignity in benedictions, for the amplitude of either discipline to be furnished, both for following the benediction and for forestalling the malediction. For so too he had premised: "Behold, I have set before you a blessing and a curse." Which he portended also into this arrangement of the gospel. Otherwise, what kind of one is he who, to insinuate his own goodness, opposed the harshness of the Creator? Weak is the commendation which is propped on the destruction of another. And yet by opposing the harshness of the Creator he confirmed him one to be feared. If to be feared, surely the rather to be obeyed than neglected; and Marcion's Christ now begins to teach men toward the Creator. Then, if the "Woe" is the Creator's, which looks toward the rich, then Christ is not offended at the rich, but the Creator, and Christ holds ratified the cases of the rich — pride I mean, and glory, and worldly pursuits, and carelessness of God, through which they deserve a "Woe" from the Creator. But how should it not belong to the same one to reprobate the rich who above approved the beggars? Everyone reprobates the contrary of that which he has approved. And so if a malediction against the rich is to be reckoned to the Creator, the benediction of the same upon the beggars will be defended, and the whole work is now the Christ of the Creator's. If the benediction upon the beggars is ascribed to the god of Marcion, the malediction upon the rich too will be imposed upon the same, and he will now be the equal of the Creator, as good as he is judge; nor will there now be room for the distinction by which two gods are made, and, the distinction removed, it will remain to announce one god the Creator. Therefore, if "Woe" is the voice either of malediction or of some sterner outcry, and is directed by Christ against the rich, I must prove the Creator the spurner of the rich too, just as I have proved him the advocate of the beggars, so that I may show Christ in this opinion too the Creator's — who enriched Solomon. But because, leave being given him to choose, he rather asked for those things which he knew pleasing to God, wisdom, he had deserved to obtain riches too, which he willed no more than that. Although it is not unbefitting for God to furnish riches too, by which both the rich are helped with comfort and many works of justice and love are administered thence. But the accidental vices of riches assign that "Woe" upon the rich in your gospel too, "Because," it says, "you have received your consolation" — surely out of riches, from their glory and their secular fruits. And so in Deuteronomy Moses says, "Lest, when thou hast eaten and been filled and built great houses, thy cattle and oxen multiplied and thy money and gold, thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the Lord thy God." Just as he assails Hezekiah too, a king puffed up with treasures and glorying in them rather than in God, before those who had come from Persia, through Isaiah: "Behold, days come, and all that is in thy house shall be taken away, and what thy fathers laid up shall be transferred to Babylon." So too through Jeremiah he published, "Let not the rich glory in his riches, and let him who glories" — namely in God — "glory." So too he inveighs against the daughters of Zion through Isaiah, puffed up with adornment and abundance of riches, threatening also elsewhere against the noble and proud: "Hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth, and the renowned and the great and the rich shall descend" (this will be Christ's "Woe" upon the rich), "and man shall be humbled" — surely exalted by riches — "and a man shall be dishonoured" — surely honourable on account of his substance. Concerning whom again: "Behold, the Lord of powers shall confound the glorious with might, and the lifted up shall be brought low, and the lofty shall fall by the sword." Who more than the rich? — because they have received their consolation, glory and honour, loftiness out of riches. From whom turning us away, in the 48th psalm too, "Fear not," he says, "when a man has been made rich, and when his glory abounds; because when he dies, he shall take nothing, nor shall his glory descend with him." Likewise in the 61st: "Desire not riches, and if they shine, set not your heart." This very word "Woe," lastly, was of old destined through Amos against the rich flowing in delights. "For woe," he says, "to those who sleep in ivory beds and flow in delights on their couches, who eat kids from the flocks of she-goats and suckling calves from the herds of oxen, applauding to the sound of instruments — they have reckoned these as things abiding and not as things fleeting — who drink strained wine and are anointed with the choicest ointments." Therefore, even if I should show the Creator only dehorting from riches, not also pre-condemning the rich — even by the very word with which Christ does — no one would doubt that the threatening upon the rich through Christ's "Woe" was added by the same one from whom the dehortation from the very matters, that is, from riches, had run before. For threatening is an accession to dehortation. He drives in a "Woe" upon the filled too, because they shall hunger; upon those who laugh now too, because they shall mourn. To these will answer those things which above were opposed to the benedictions with the Creator: "Behold, those who serve me shall be filled, but you shall hunger" — surely because you are filled; "and behold, those who serve me shall be delighted, but you shall be confounded" — surely about to weep, who now laugh. For just as in the psalm, "Those who sow in tears shall reap in gladness," so in the gospel, "Those who sow in laughter" — namely out of gladness — "shall reap in tears." These things the Creator of old set together; Christ, only by distinguishing, not by changing, renewed them. "Woe, when men shall bless you. For after these things did their fathers to the false prophets too." Equally the Creator accuses the followers of human benediction and praise through Isaiah: "My people, those who call you blessed seduce you and disturb the ways of your feet." He forbids elsewhere to trust at all in man, so also in the praise of man, as through Jeremiah: "Cursed is the man who has hope in man." For also in the 117th psalm: "It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man, and it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes." Thus the Creator forswore all that is caught from man, much more benediction. But to reproach false prophets praised or blessed by their fathers is as much his as to reproach prophets harassed and refused: just as the injuries of the prophets would not have pertained to their god, so neither would the favours toward the false prophets have displeased any but the god of the prophets.

16. "But I say to you," he says, "who hear" (showing this commanded of old by the Creator, "Speak in the ears of those who hear"), "love your enemies, and bless those who hate you, and pray for those who calumniate you." These the Creator shut up in one pronouncement through Isaiah: "Say, You are our brothers, to those who hate you." For if those who are enemies and hate and curse and calumniate are to be called brothers, surely he too commanded the haters to be blessed and the calumniators to be prayed for, who enjoined that they be reckoned brothers. Plainly Christ teaches a new patience, restraining even the requital of injury permitted by the Creator, who demands an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; on the contrary he himself bids the other cheek besides be offered, and that the cloak too be yielded over the tunic. Plainly these things Christ added as supplements consonant with the discipline of the Creator. And so this is at once to be reported — whether the discipline of patience is proclaimed with the Creator. He commanded through Zechariah that no one should remember the malice of his brother, but not even of his neighbour. For again, "The malice of his neighbour," it says, "let no one reconsider." Much more did he indict patience under injury who indicted forgetfulness. But also when he says, "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay," he accordingly teaches a patience that awaits vengeance. Inasmuch, then, as it does not gain credit that the same one should seem both to demand a tooth for a tooth, an eye for an eye, in requital of injury, who not only forbids requital but even vengeance, even the recollection and reconsideration of injury — by so much is it opened to us how he ordained an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, not to permit a second injury of retaliation, which he had forbidden by interdicting vengeance, but to coerce the first, which he had forbidden by the retaliation set against it — so that each one, regarding the licence of a second injury, might contain himself from the first. For he knows that violence is more easily compressed by the representation of retaliation than by the promise of vengeance. But both had to be appointed for the nature and the faith of men, that he who believed God might await vengeance from God, while he who had less faith might fear the laws of retaliation. This will of the law, labouring under the understanding, the Lord both of the sabbath and of the law and of all the paternal arrangements, Christ, both revealed and made effective, commanding the offering of the other cheek too, that he might the more extinguish the requital of injury which the law too had wished to impede through retaliation — certainly which prophecy had manifestly coerced, both forbidding the memory of injury and reducing vengeance to God. Thus if Christ brought in anything, not by an adversary's but by a helper's precept, he did not destroy the disciplines of the Creator. In short, if I consider the very reason of this patience to be enjoined — and that so full and perfect — it will not stand, if he is not the Creator's who promises vengeance, who furnishes a judge. Otherwise, if so great a weight of patience — of not only not striking back but even offering the other cheek, and not only not cursing back but even blessing, and not only not retaining the tunic but even granting the cloak besides — is imposed on me by one who is not to defend me, he commanded patience to no purpose, not exhibiting to me the reward of the precept, the fruit of patience I mean, which is vengeance, which he ought to have permitted me, if he furnishes it not himself, or, if he did not permit it me, to furnish it himself; since it concerns discipline too that injury be avenged. For by fear of vengeance all iniquity is bridled. But, licence being sent forth at large, it will domineer, gouging out both eyes and rousing every tooth in the security of impunity. But this belongs to a best and only good god — to suffer injury to patience, to set open the door to violence, not to defend the upright, not to coerce the wicked. "Give to everyone that asks thee" — surely to the needy, or so much the more to the needy, even though to the abounding too. Lest, then, anyone be needy, you have for the giver a form commanded in Deuteronomy by the Creator. "There shall not be," it says, "in thee a needy man, that blessing he may bless thee, the Lord thy God" — the giver, namely, who shall have caused that there be no needy one. And more here. For he does not bid give to the asker. But "let there not be," he says, "a needy man in thee," that is, take care beforehand that there be not; whereby he the more prejudges that it must be given to the asker, even in what follows. "But if there be a needy man among thy brothers, thou shalt not turn away thy heart, nor close thy hand from a needy brother. Opening thou shalt open thy hand to him, lending thou shalt lend to him as much as he desires." For a loan is not wont to be given but to one who asks. But concerning the loan afterward. Now if anyone wish to argue that the Creator indeed bade give to brothers, but Christ to all who ask, so that this is new and diverse — nay, it will be one of those things through which the law of the Creator will be in Christ. For Christ commanded toward all no other thing than what the Creator did toward brothers. For even though the goodness is greater which works toward strangers, yet it is not prior to that which ought first toward neighbours. For who shall be able to love strangers? But if the second degree of goodness is toward strangers, which toward neighbours is the first, the second degree will belong to the same one whose is the first too, more easily than that the second should be his whose the first did not exist. Thus the Creator both, according to the order of nature, taught benignity first toward neighbours, intending to send it forth afterward toward strangers, and, according to the reason of his arrangement, first toward the Jews, afterward toward all the human race too. And therefore, so long as the mystery was within Israel, with reason he commanded mercy upon brothers alone; but when to Christ he gave the nations for an inheritance and the ends of the earth for a possession, and that began to be discharged which was said through Hosea, "Not my people, my people, and she that has not obtained mercy, having obtained mercy" — namely the nation — then Christ extended toward all the law of the paternal benignity, excepting no one in commiseration, as none in vocation. Thus even if he taught anything more, this too he received into the inheritance of the nations. "And as you wish men to do to you, so do you also to them." In this precept surely the other part of it is understood: "And as you do not wish men to do to you, so do you also not do to them." If a new and hitherto unknown god and not yet plainly published commanded this, who had formed me by no prior institution, by which I might first know what I ought to wish or not wish for myself, and so do to others what I should wish for myself, and not do what I should not wish for myself — he permitted my opinion to be promiscuous, and did not bind me to a conformity of will and deed, so that I should do to others what I should wish for myself and should not do to others what I should not wish for myself. For he did not define what I ought to wish or not wish for myself and for others, so that, to a law of will I might match my deed, and might both not furnish to another what I should wish furnished to me by another — love, obedience, comfort, protection, and such goods — and likewise do to another what I should not wish done to me by another — violence, injury, contumely, fraud, and such evils. In short, by this inconformity of will and deed act the ethnics, not yet instructed by God. For even if good and evil are known by nature, yet not the discipline of God, by which known, then at last a conformity of will and deed out of faith, as under the fear of God, is enacted. And so the god of Marcion, though most fully revealed, yet, revealed, could not have sent forth a compendium of this precept of which we treat, so strict and obscure and still blind and the more easily to be interpreted according to my own choice rather — of which he had built up beforehand no distinction. But my Creator both of old and everywhere commanded the needy, the poor and orphans and widows, to be protected, helped, refreshed; as also through Isaiah: "Break thy bread to the beggars, and those who are without a roof bring into thy house, and if thou see one naked, cover him." Likewise through Ezekiel, of the just man: "His bread he shall give to the hungry, and shall cover the naked." Sufficiently, then, even then he taught me to do to others those things which I should wish done to me. Accordingly, denouncing, "Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness," he taught me not to do to others what I should not wish done to me; and therefore the precept in the gospel will belong to him who both built it up beforehand and distinguished it and arranged it according to the choice of his discipline, and now with reason has bound it up in a compendium — since in other respects too the Lord, that is Christ, was proclaimed as one who would make a curtailed word upon the earth.

17. Here now, when he interposes concerning the loan, "And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what grace is it to you?" run through what follows in Ezekiel concerning the same just man: "His money," it says, "he has not given for usury, and what abounds he will not take" — the redundancy of the loan, namely, which is interest. First, then, it was that he should root out the fruit of the loan, that he might the more easily accustom a man to lose even the very loan, if at all, whose fruit he had learned to forgo. For this we say was the work of the law, providing for the gospel. The faith of certain men then, little by little, toward the perfect lustre of Christian discipline, it was forming by those first precepts of a benignity still stammering. For above too, "And the pledge," it says, "thou shalt restore to the giver" — surely if he be not able to pay, since to a payer the pledge would in any case be restored without his writing it. Much more manifestly in Deuteronomy: "Thou shalt not sleep upon his pledge; restoring thou shalt restore to him his cloak about the setting of the sun, and he shall sleep in his cloak." More clearly still above: "Thou shalt remit every debt which thy neighbour owes thee, and thy brother thou shalt not demand back, because the remission of the Lord thy God has been invoked." Now when he bids the debt be remitted, surely to one not about to pay (for it is more, even if he be about to pay, when he forbids it to be demanded back), what else does he teach than that we should lend to one not about to pay, who indicted so great a loss upon the loan? "And you shall be sons of God." Nothing more shameless, if he shall make us sons to himself who did not permit us to make sons by taking away marriage. How will he draw his own into that name which he has already erased? I cannot be the son of a eunuch, especially when I have the same Father whom even the universe has. For he is as much the Father of all, being the founder of the universe, as a eunuch is the founder of no substance. And even if the Creator had not mingled male and female, even if he had not granted sons to all the animals too, this I was of his before paradise, before delinquency, before exile, before the two were one. Anew I was made a son, straightway when he brought me forth with his hands, when he moved me with his breath. He now again names me son, begetting me now not into a soul, but into a spirit. "Because he," it says, "is sweet toward the ungrateful and evil." Well done, Marcion; ingeniously enough you took from him the rains and suns, lest the Creator should appear. But who is this sweet one, who has not even hitherto been known? How sweet, from whom no benefits of this kind of sweetness, of suns and rains, had preceded, who had lent them? — one not about to receive again from the human race, like the Creator, who, for so great a liberality of the elements, still bears with men rendering the debt of gratitude more readily to idols than to himself. Truly sweet even in spiritual commodities. For "the utterances of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycombs." He, then, censured the ungrateful too who deserved to find men grateful, whose sun and rains even you, Marcion, held in ingratitude. But yours could not now complain of the ungrateful, who had not prepared grateful ones. Commanding mercy too, "Be," he says, "merciful, as your Father has had mercy on you." This will be, "Break thy bread to the hungry, and those without a roof bring into thy house, and if thou see one naked, cover him," and, "Judge the orphan, and justify the widow." I acknowledge his old teaching, who prefers mercy to sacrifice. Or if another has now commanded mercy, because he himself too is merciful, why was he not merciful to me for so great an age? "Do not judge, lest you be judged. Do not condemn, lest you be condemned. Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you — a good measure, pressed down and overflowing, they shall give into your bosom. With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you." As I think, these things sound a retribution provoked according to merits. From whom, then, the retribution? If from men only, then he teaches a human discipline and reward, and we shall obey men altogether: if from the Creator, as from a judge and assessor of merits, then he impels our obedience toward him with whom he has appointed the retribution to be caught at or feared, according as each shall have judged or condemned or forgiven or measured: if from himself, then he too now judges, which Marcion denies. Let the Marcionites therefore choose whether it be worth so much to fall away from the rule of their master as it is worth to have a Christ teaching either for men or for the Creator. But the blind leads the blind into the pit. Some believe Marcion. But the disciple is not above his master. This Apelles ought to have remembered, the emendator of the disciple Marcion. Let the heretic too take the beam out of his own eye, then let him censure, if any, the straw he thinks in the eye of the Christian. Accordingly the good tree too does not bring forth evil fruit, because neither does truth heresy, nor the evil good, because neither does heresy truth. So neither did Marcion bring forth anything good out of the evil treasure of Cerdo, nor Apelles out of Marcion's. For much more congruently shall we interpret of these men those things which Christ allegorized of men, not of two gods according to the scandal of Marcion. I think I am not rashly insisting thus far still upon this line, by which I define that nowhere at all was another god revealed by Christ. In this one adultery I marvel that the hand of Marcion grew numb. Unless that even robbers are afraid. No misdeed is without dread, because neither without consciousness of itself. So long, then, did the Jews too know no other god than him besides whom they knew none as yet, nor call any other god than him whom alone they knew. If it is so, who will seem to have said, "Why do you call me, Lord, Lord?" Either he who had never been so called, as one nowhere as yet published, or he who was always held to be Lord, as known from the beginning, the god of the Jews, namely? Who likewise could have added, "And do not do what I say?" Either he who at that moment was trying to teach, or he who from the beginning had committed to them the utterances both of the law and the prophets? Who could also reproach them with disobedience, even if he had never reproached them otherwise? Now he who before Christ harangued, "This people loves me with their lips, but their heart stands far off from me," surely imputed to them an old contumacy. Otherwise, how absurd, that a new god, a new Christ, the illuminator of a new and so great a religion, should pronounce contumacious and disobedient those whom he could not have tried.

18. Likewise, the faith of the centurion being extolled, it is incredible if he professed that he had found no such faith even in Israel, to whom the faith of Israel did not pertain. But neither thence could it have pertained, still raw to be proved or compared, not to say still none. But why should it not have been lawful for him to use the example of an alien faith? Because, if it were so, he would have said that such faith had never even been in Israel; but in saying that such faith he ought to have found in Israel — he indeed who had come for this, that he might find it, namely the god and the Christ of Israel — he would not have censured it but as the exactor and follower of it. But a rival would even have preferred it found such, for the weakening and destroying of which he had rather come, not for the approving. He raised up too the dead son of the widow. No new evidence. This even the prophets of the Creator had put forth; how much more the Son? But so far up to that moment had the Lord Christ brought in no other god, that they all there rendered glory to the Creator, saying, "A great prophet has come forth among us, and God has regarded his people." What god? Surely whose the people was, and from whom the prophets. But if they indeed glorified the Creator, while Christ both hearing and knowing did not correct them — and that in so great an evidence of a dead man raised up, still praying to the Creator — without doubt either he carried about no other god than him whom he suffered to be honoured in his own benefits and powers, or what kind of thing is it that he suffered them so long to err, having come for this, that he might heal their error? But John is scandalized at hearing of the powers of Christ, as of another's. But I will first explain the reason of the scandal, that I may the more easily explode the heretic's scandal. The Lord of powers being now himself, the Word and the Spirit of the Father working on earth and preaching, it was necessary that the portion of the Holy Spirit — which, after the form of a prophetic measure, had wrought in John the preparation of the Lord's ways — should now withdraw from John, reduced, namely, into the Lord, as into its own mass-sum. And so John, now a common man, and now one of the crowd, was scandalized indeed as a man, but not as one hoping for or understanding another Christ, who would neither hope for the same one as teaching or working nothing new. No one will hesitate concerning someone whom, while he knows him not to exist, he neither hopes for nor understands; but John was certain of no god besides the Creator, both as a Jew and as a prophet. Plainly he hesitated, as it were, about one whom, though he knew him to exist, whether he himself were he he knew not. By this fear, then, John too: "Art thou," he says, "he that cometh, or do we look for another?" — simply inquiring whether he himself had come whom he was awaiting. "Art thou he that cometh," that is, who art to come, "or do we look for another?" — that is, is there another whom we look for, if thou art not he whom we look for as to come? For he hoped, as all supposed, that from a likeness of the evidences a prophet too might meanwhile have been sent, from whom another should be, that is, greater — the very Lord, namely, who was awaited as to come. And this then was John's scandal, that he doubted whether he himself had come whom they awaited, whom they ought to have acknowledged also by the proclaimed operations — so that the Lord announced to John that he was to be acknowledged through those same operations. And since these are established to have been proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator, as we have shown at each point, it is perverse enough that by those things he should have announced that a Christ not of the Creator was to be understood, through which he the rather compelled the Christ of the Creator to be acknowledged. Much more perverse, if the Christ who was not John's bears testimony to John, confirming him a prophet — nay, even above as an angel — driving in too what was written concerning him: "Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way" — elegantly, toward the former sense of the scandalized John, commemorating the prophecy, that, confirming the forerunner John already to have come, he might extinguish the scruple of that interrogation, "Art thou he that cometh, or do we look for another?" For, the forerunner having now discharged his office, the way of the Lord prepared, he himself was to be understood, to whom the forerunner had ministered — greater indeed than all born of women, but not therefore subject to him who should be lesser in the kingdom of God; as though the kingdom were of one god in which someone modest shall be greater than John, and John, who is greater than all born of women, of another. For whether he speaks, through humility, of someone modest, or of himself, because he was held lesser than John — all, namely, running together into the wilderness to John rather than to Christ ("What did you go out into the wilderness to see?") — equally it both befits the Creator both that John is greater than all born of women, and that Christ, or any modest one, should be greater than John in the kingdom equally of the Creator, and that he who was not scandalized at Christ — which then made John less — should be greater than so great a prophet. We have spoken concerning remission of sins. But the argument of that sinful woman will tend hither: that, when she fastened with kisses the feet of the Lord, inundated them with tears, wiped them with her hair, smeared them with ointment, she handled the truth of a solid body, not an empty phantom; and that the penitence of the sinner deserved pardon according to the Creator, accustomed to prefer it to sacrifice. But also, if the goad of penitence had come by faith, through penitence justified by faith she heard from him, "Thy faith has made thee safe," who through Habakkuk had pronounced, "The just shall live by his faith."

19. That rich women clung to Christ, who ministered to him out of their faculties, among whom too the wife of the king's procurator — this is from prophecy. For these Isaiah called rich women: "Arise and hear my voice," that he might show them first as disciples, then as workers and ministers: "Daughters in hope, hear my words: in the day of the year remember with labour in hope"; for with labour, by which they followed, and on account of hope, they ministered. Equally, concerning parables, let it suffice once for all to have proved this kind of speech promised by the Creator. But now that pronouncement of his too to the people, "With the ear you shall hear, and shall not hear," gave Christ occasion frequently to inculcate, "He that has ears, let him hear." Not as though, out of diversity, Christ permitted a hearing which the Creator had taken away, but because exhortation followed the threat. First, "With the ear you shall hear, and shall not hear"; then, "He that has ears, let him hear." For they did not hear spontaneously who had ears, but he showed the ears of the heart necessary, with which the Creator had denied they would hear. And therefore through Christ he adds: "See how you hear, and do not hear" — not hearing, namely, with the heart, but with the ear. If you accommodate a worthy sense to the pronouncement, in place of the sense of him who roused them to a hearing, even by saying, "See how you hear," he was threatening those who would not hear. To be sure, the most mild god threatens, since he neither judges nor grows angry! This the underlying sense too proves. "To him who has it shall be given, but from him who has not, even what he thinks he has shall be taken from him." What shall be given? An increase of faith, or of understanding, or salvation itself. What shall be taken? Surely what is given. By whom is it given and taken? If by the Creator it is taken, by him it is also given. If by the god of Marcion it is given, by him it is also taken. By whatever name, however, he threatens a taking-away, it will not belong to that god who knows not how to threaten, because he knows not how to be angry. I marvel, however, when he denies that a lamp is wont to be hidden, who hid himself for so great an age — a greater and more necessary light; when he promises all things from the hidden to the open, who darkens his god even to this point, awaiting, I suppose, the birth of Marcion. We come to the most constant argument of all who bring the Lord's nativity into controversy. "He himself," they say, "attests that he was not born, by saying, 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?'" Thus the heretics always either snatch bare and simple voices by conjecture whither they will, or again dissolve conditional and rational ones by the condition of simplicity, as in this place. We on the contrary say, first, that it could not have been announced to him that his mother and his brothers stood outside seeking to see him, if there were no mother to him and no brothers — whom surely he knew who announced them, either formerly known or then and there ascertained, while they desire to see him, or while they themselves send the message. To this our first proposition it is wont to be answered from the opposite side: "What, if it was announced to him for the sake of tempting him?" But this the Scripture does not say, which, in so far as it is wont to signify that something was done out of temptation ("Behold, a doctor of the law rose up tempting him," and concerning the consultation about tribute, "And the Pharisees came to him tempting him"), in so far, where it does not make mention of temptation, it does not admit the interpretation of temptation. And yet, over and above, I demand the reasons of the temptation — for what they tempted him by the naming of mother and brothers. If that they might know whether he had been born or not — when was there a question of this which from that temptation they should discuss? And who would doubt to have been born one whom he saw a man? whom he had heard profess himself the Son of man? whom from the aspect of all human quality he would doubt to believe God or the Son of God? — esteeming him more easily a prophet, even some great one, yet surely born? Even if in the exploration of his nativity he had been to be tempted, any other argument would have suited the temptation than through the mention of those persons whom even one born might not have. Tell me, does the mother survive for all the born? are brothers begotten besides for all the born? Is it not rather lawful to have fathers and sisters, or even no one? But also it is established that censuses were taken under Augustus then in Judea by Sentius Saturninus, among whom they could have inquired his lineage. So in no way did the reason of that temptation stand, and truly his mother and brothers stood outside. It remains also to inspect the sense of one not pronouncing simply, "Who is my mother or brothers?" as toward a denial of his lineage and nativity, but both out of the necessity of the case and from a rational condition. For that persons so near should stand outside, while strangers were fixed within upon his discourse, and besides seeking to call him away from his solemn work — with reason was he indignant. He did not so much abnegate as disavow. And so, when he had premised, "Who is my mother and who are my brothers?" subjoining, "Except those who hear my words and do them," he transferred the names of blood to others, whom he would judge nearer for their faith. But no one transfers a thing except from him who has that which he transfers. If, then, he made his mother and brothers those who were not such, how did he deny those who were? — on the condition, namely, of merits, not out of a denial of his near ones — teaching in himself that he who should prefer father or mother or brothers to the word of God is not a worthy disciple. For the rest, from this he the rather confessed his mother and brothers, in that he was unwilling to acknowledge them. In that he adopted others, he confirmed those whom out of offence he denied — for whom he substituted not truer ones, but worthier. In short, it is nothing great, if he preferred faith to blood, which he did not have.

20. But who is this who commands both the winds and the sea? Surely a new commander and possessor of the elements, the Creator being already subdued and shut out? It is not so. But the substances acknowledged their author, who had been wont to obey his servants too. Look into Exodus, Marcion; behold the rod of Moses commanding the Red Sea — vaster beyond all the pools of Judea — that, cleft to the bottom and fixed with equal astonishment of the parting on either side, it should let the people across with dry foot by a path through its midst; and again, nature returning at the nod of the same rod, that it should overwhelm the Egyptian army by the concord of the waters — to which work the south winds too gave service. Read that to the exiled family, when it was to be parted, in its crossing, the Jordan was a sword, whose impetus and current Joshua too had plainly taught to stand still as the prophets passed over. What of these? If your Christ is meant, he will not be more powerful than the servants of the Creator. But I should have used these examples alone, had not the proclamation of this marine expedition too preceded Christ. For when he crosses, the psalm is discharged. "The Lord," it says, "upon many waters." When he shakes the waves of the strait, Habakkuk is fulfilled. "Scattering," it says, "the waters by his journey." When at his threats the sea is dashed away, Nahum too is performed. "Threatening," it says, "the sea and drying it up" — surely with the winds, by which it was disquieted. Whence do you wish my Christ to be vindicated — from the examples, or from the prophets of the Creator? Come now, you who think that a soldierly and armed warrior is foretold, not figuratively nor allegorically — one who was to wage a spiritual war against spiritual enemies with spiritual soldiery and spiritual arms, spiritually — when you find in one man a multitude of demons, professing itself a legion, surely a spiritual one, learn too that Christ is to be understood the expugner of spiritual enemies, spiritually armed and spiritually warlike, and so that he himself it is who was to fight with a legion of demons too; so that of this war too the psalm may seem to have pronounced, "The Lord strong, the Lord mighty in war." For when he fought with the last enemy, death, through the trophy of the cross he triumphed. But whose god's son did the legion attest Jesus to be? Without doubt his whose torments and abyss they knew and feared. For neither do they seem to have been able as yet to be ignorant that a power of a new and unknown god was working on earth, because it is not likely that the Creator was ignorant. For if he had once been ignorant of another god above himself, yet now surely he had discovered one acting beneath his own heaven. But what the Lord had discovered would now have become known to the whole household too, in the same world and within the same circuit of heaven in which a foreign divinity was conversing. Inasmuch, then, as the Creator too would have known it, and the substance of it, if it had existed — by so much, because there was none, the demons knew no other than the Christ of their own god. For they do not seek from another what they would remember should be sought by them from the Creator, namely pardon of the abyss of the Creator. In short, they obtained it. By what desert? Because they had lied, because they had made him the son of a fierce god? And what kind of one will he be who helped liars, who suffered defamers? But because they had not lied, because they had known the god of the abyss and their own, so he too confirmed himself the one whom the demons had known, Jesus the judge and the son of the avenging god. Behold something too concerning those littlenesses and infirmities of the Creator in Christ. For I too wish to ascribe ignorance to him. Permit me, against a heretic. He is touched by a woman who flowed with blood, and he knew not by whom. "Who," he says, "touched me?" Even when the disciples make excuse, he persists in the voice of ignorance. "Someone touched me," and this he affirms from argument. "For I felt power gone out from me." What says the heretic? Did he know the person? And why did he speak as one ignorant? To provoke confession, certainly; to prove fear. So too Adam once was sought, as one ignorant, "Adam, where art thou?" You have both the Creator excused along with Christ, and Christ equated with the Creator. But also that, as an adversary of the law — that, because the law removes from the touch of a bleeding woman, therefore he desired not only to admit her touch but even to grant soundness. O a god beneficent not by nature, but by rivalry! But indeed, if we find the woman's faith to have so deserved, when he says, "Thy faith has made thee safe," who are you, to interpret a rivalry of the law in that deed which the Lord himself showed to have been put forth out of the reward of faith? But you wish to constitute this the woman's faith, by which she had despised the law. And to whom is it credible that a woman, conscious as yet of no god, initiated as yet into no new law, should burst into that law by which she was still held? By what faith, in short, did she burst in? believing in what god? despising whom? The Creator? Certainly out of faith she touched. If out of faith in the Creator, who knew no other god, how did she burst into his law? For she burst in, if she burst in, as much out of faith in the Creator. For how shall both agree, both that she burst in, and that out of faith she burst into that on account of which she ought not to have burst in? I will tell. This faith was first that by which she trusted that her own god preferred mercy to sacrifice itself, by which she was certain that he wrought in Christ, by which she so touched him, not as a holy man, nor as a prophet, whom she knew contaminable by reason of human substance, but as the very god, whom she had presumed no filth could pollute. And so she did not rashly interpret the law for herself, signifying that those things were contaminated which were contaminable, not the god, whom she trusted in Christ. But she reconsidered this too, that the ordinary and solemn flux of menstrual or natal blood is taxed in the law, which comes from an office of nature, not from a defect of health. But she was redundant from a defect of health, for whom she knew necessary not the measure of time, but the help of the divine mercy. And so she can seem not to have burst into the law, but to have distinguished it. This will be the faith which had conferred understanding too. "Unless you believe," it says, "you shall not understand." This faith of that woman, who believed only the Creator, Christ approving, answered himself to be the god of that faith which he approved. Nor will I omit that, while his garment is touched — surely a garment put upon a body, not a phantom — a body too was demonstrated; not as though we should now treat of this, but because it conspires to the present question. For if there was no truth of body, surely the phantom, as an empty thing, could not be contaminated. He, then, who cannot be contaminated by reason of the emptiness of substance, how could he have wished to be? As an adversary of the law he was lying, who was not truly polluted.

21. He sends the disciples to preach the kingdom of God. Did he even here publish whose? He forbids them to carry anything for food or clothing on the way. Who would have commanded this but he who both feeds the ravens and clothes the flowers of the field, who before granted to the ox too treading out the grain freedom of mouth for the pardon of fodder, in removing it from the work, because the worker is worthy of his hire? Let Marcion delete these, provided the sense be safe. But when he bids the dust be shaken off the feet upon those by whom they had not been received, and commands this too to be done for a testimony — no one testifies what is not destined for judgement; he who bids inhumanity be reduced to a testimony threatens a judge. That no new god was approved by Christ that opinion too of all declared, because some asserted to Herod that Christ Jesus was John, others Elias, others some one of the old prophets. Of whom whichever it had been, surely not for this was he raised up, that after the resurrection he should preach another god. He feeds the people in the wilderness, namely after the former manner. Or if it is not the same majesty, then he is already lesser than the Creator, who not in one day, but in forty years, nor out of the inferior matters of bread and fish, but out of heavenly manna, nor about five, but six hundred thousand men supported. And so far was it majesty, that he willed even a scantiness of food not only to suffice but even to overflow, from the former example. For so too in the time of famine under Elias the scanty and last food of the Sareptan widow, out of the prophet's blessing, had abounded through the whole time of famine. You have the third book of Kingdoms. If you unfold the fourth too, you will find this whole order of Christ about that man of God who, when ten barley loaves had been offered him, bade them be distributed with the people, and his minister, accordingly considering the multitude and the smallness of the food, had answered, "What should I give of this in the sight of a hundred men?" "Give," he says, "and they shall eat, because thus says the Lord, They shall eat and shall leave remnants, according to the word of the Lord." O Christ, old even in the new! These things, then, Peter, who had seen them and had compared them with the former, and had recognized not only things formerly done, but things even then prophesying for the future — when, the Lord inquiring who he seemed to them to be, he answered for all, "Thou art the Christ" — could not but have understood him Christ, none other than the one he had known in the Scriptures, whom he was now recounting in deeds. This he himself too confirms, still patient — nay, even enjoining silence. For if Peter indeed could confess him no other than the Creator's, while he commanded them to tell this to no one, surely he was unwilling that to be divulged which Peter had perceived. "Nay," you say, "because he had not perceived rightly, he was unwilling a lie to be disseminated." But he declared another cause of the silence, that the Son of man must suffer many things, and be reprobated by elders and scribes and priests, and be killed, and after the third day rise again. Which things, since they too are proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator — as we shall fulfil in their places — even thus he showed himself to be the very one concerning whom they were proclaimed. Certainly, even if they had not been proclaimed, he brought forth as the cause of the enjoined silence one which should demonstrate not Peter's error, but the necessity of the passions to be undergone. "Whoever," he says, "shall wish to make his soul safe, shall lose it; and whoever shall lose it for my sake, shall make it safe." Certainly the Son of man uttered this opinion. Look, then, you too, with the king of Babylon, into his burning furnace, and you will find there, as it were the Son of man (for he was not yet truly so, namely not yet born of man), even then constituting these issues. He makes safe the souls of the three brothers, who had conspired to lose them for God, but lost those of the Chaldeans, which they had preferred to make safe through idolatry. What is this new teaching, of which the evidences are old? Although the proclamations of martyrdoms too, both as to come and as to bring a reward from God, ran their course. "See," says Isaiah, "how the just man perishes, and no one takes it to heart, and just men are taken away, and no one considers." When more is this done than in the persecution of his saints? Surely not a simple loss, nor a common one by the law of nature, but that signal and warlike-for-faith one, in which he who loses his soul for God saves it — that here too you may acknowledge a judge, who recompenses the evil gain of the soul by its loss, and the good loss of the soul by its salvation. But he exhibits to me a jealous god too, repaying evil with evil. "Whoever," he says, "shall have been confounded at me, I too will be confounded at him." Since the matter of confusion would suit none but my Christ, whose order is the more to be blushed at — so that it lies open even to the revilings of heretics, who harangue with all the bitterness they can about the whole foulness of his nativity and rearing and even the very indignity of his flesh — for the rest, how shall he be liable to confusion who does not admit it? — coagulated not, indeed, in a virgin's womb, yet in a woman's, and even if not of seed, yet by the law of corporeal substance, out of the humour of a woman; not held flesh before its shaping, not called a beast after its figuring, not deliberated through ten months' torment, not poured out to the earth in a sudden shaking of pangs along with the mire of so long a time through the sewer of the body, nor at once auspicating the light with tears and the first wound of his own swaddling, nor much washed, nor medicated with salt and honey, nor first wrapped in the cerements that are already a burial-cloth, nor thence rolled through filth among the bosoms, troublesome to the breasts, long an infant, scarcely a boy, slowly a man — but set forth from heaven, at once grown, at once whole, straightway Christ, only spirit and power and god. For the rest, as not true, who was not seen, so neither to be blushed at for the curse of the cross, of which he lacked the truth, lacking the body. He could not therefore have said, "Whoever shall have been confounded at me." Ours ought to have pronounced this — diminished by the Father a little below the angels, a worm and not a man, the shame of man and the outcast of the people — inasmuch as he so willed it, that by his bruise we should be healed, that by his dishonour our salvation should stand. And with reason he laid himself down for his own man, for his own image and likeness, not another's; that, since man had not blushed to adore stone and wood, with the same constancy, not confounded at Christ, he might make satisfaction to God for the shamelessness of idolatry through the shamelessness of faith. Which of these suits your Christ, Marcion, to the desert of confusion? Plainly you ought to be ashamed that you yourself fashioned him.

22. For this too you ought to have blushed at most of all, that you allow him to be seen with Moses and Elias on the retirement of the mountain, whose destroyer he had come. This, namely, that voice from heaven willed to be understood, "This is my beloved Son, hear him" — that is, no longer Moses and Elias. Therefore the voice alone sufficed, without the showing of Moses and Elias. For by defining whom they should hear, he would have forbidden any others to be heard. Or perhaps did he permit Isaiah and Jeremiah and the rest, whom he did not show, to be heard, if he forbade those whom he showed? Now even if their presence was necessary, surely they would not be shown in colloquy, which is a sign of familiarity, nor in a fellowship of brightness, which is an example of esteem and grace, but in some foulness, which is an argument of destruction — nay, in the darkness of the Creator, for the dispelling of which he had been sent — far removed too from the brightness of Christ, who was to separate even their voices and letters from his gospel. Thus he demonstrates them aliens while he has them with him. Thus he teaches that they are to be left whom he joins to himself. Thus he destroys those whom he builds up out of his own rays. What would the Christ of those men do? I believe, according to the perversity, he would have revealed them such as Marcion's Christ ought to have been, or any others with him than his own prophets. But what is so the Christ of the Creator's as to show his own preachers with himself? to be seen with those to whom in revelations he had been seen? to speak with those who had spoken him? to share his glory with those by whom he was named the Lord of glory? — with his own chief men, of whom the one was once the informer of the people, the other one day the reformer, the one the initiator of the old testament, the other the consummator of the new. And so Peter too, with reason acknowledging the comradeship of his own Christ by the individuality of his presence, suggests counsel: "It is good for us to be here" (good plainly where Moses, namely, and Elias are), and, "Let us make here three tabernacles, one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias"; but not knowing what he said. How not knowing? Either through simple error, or by that reason by which we defend, in the cause of the new prophecy, that ecstasy — that is, a being out of one's mind — befits grace? For a man set in the spirit, especially when he beholds the glory of God, or when God speaks through him, must of necessity fall from his senses, overshadowed, namely, by the divine power — concerning which there is a question between us and the psychics. Meanwhile it is easy to prove the ecstasy of Peter. For how would he have known Moses and Elias, except in the spirit? (for the people could not have had their images or statues and likenesses, the law forbidding) — except that he had seen them in the spirit? And so what he had said in the spirit, not set in his senses, he could not know. For the rest, if he so knows not as one erring — in that he thought Christ to belong to them — then it is now established that above too, when Peter was interrogated by Christ whom they esteemed him to be, he said, of the Creator's, "Thou art the Christ"; because, if he had then acknowledged him to be of another god, here too he would not have erred. But if here too he therefore erred because above too, then you are certain that on that day too no new divinity was revealed by Christ, and that Peter had not yet erred, Christ hitherto revealing nothing of the kind, and that Christ was so long not to be reckoned of another than the Creator, whose whole order he here too expressed. Three of the learners he takes as witnesses of the coming vision and voice. And this is the Creator's. "In three witnesses," it says, "shall every word stand." He retires into the mountain. I acknowledge the form of the place. For the former people too the Creator had initiated at the mountain both by vision and by his voice. It behoved that upon that platform the new testament should be sealed where the old had been written, under the same circuit too of the cloud, which no one will doubt to be massed out of the Creator's air. Unless he had led even his own clouds thither, because he too had broken his way through the Creator's heaven; or else he used the Creator's cloud-cover by leave. And so neither now was the cloud mute, but the wonted voice from heaven, and the Father's new testimony over the Son, as in the first psalm: "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee." Concerning whom also through Isaiah: "Who fearing God shall hear the voice of his Son?" And so, now representing him, "This is my Son" — surely it is understood, "whom I promised." For if he promised at some time, and afterward says, "This is he," it is the part of one exhibiting to use a voice in the demonstration of the promise who at some time promised, not of one to whom it can be answered, "Who indeed art thou who sayest, This is my Son, concerning whom thou hast no more premised than that thou hast revealed thyself, which thou wast before?" Hear him therefore whom he had from the beginning declared was to be heard in the name of a prophet, since he was to be esteemed a prophet too by the people. "A prophet," says Moses, "shall God raise up to you from your sons," namely according to carnal descent, "as me; him shall you hear. But everyone who shall not hear him, his soul shall be exterminated from his people." So too Isaiah: "Who among you fearing shall hear the voice of his Son?" — which the Father himself too was to commend. For "establishing," it says, "the words of his Son," by saying, namely, "This is my beloved Son, hear him." And so, even if a transference of hearing has been made from Moses and Elias to Christ, yet not as from another god, nor to another Christ, but from the Creator to his Christ, according to the decession of the old and the succession of the new testament. "Not a legate," says Isaiah, "nor a messenger, but he himself, God, shall save them" — he himself now preaching and fulfilling the law and the prophets. The Father, then, handed over new disciples to the Son, Moses and Elias being first shown with him in the prerogative of brightness, and so dismissed, as already discharged both in office and in honour — that this very thing might be confirmed against Marcion, that there is a fellowship even of Christ's brightness with Moses and Elias. But the whole bearing of that vision we have also with Habakkuk, where the spirit, sometimes in the person of the apostles: "Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid." What rather than that of the heavenly voice: "This is my beloved Son, hear him"? "I considered thy works, and was astonished." When more than when, the brightness of him being seen, Peter knew not what he said? "In the midst of two living creatures thou shalt be known" — Moses and Elias. Concerning whom Zechariah too saw in the figure of two olives and two olive-branches. For these are they of whom it was said to him, "Two sons of fatness stand by the Lord of the whole earth." And again the same Habakkuk: "A power covered the heavens" — surely with that cloud-cover; "and his splendour shall be as the light" — surely by which his garment too shone. And if we be reminded of the promise of Moses, here it will be found discharged. For when Moses had desired the sight of the Lord, saying, "If, then, I have found grace before thee, manifest thyself to me, that knowing I may see thee" — desiring that sight in which he was to act a man, which the prophet knew — for the rest, concerning the face of God he had already heard, "No man shall see me and live." "And this word too which thou hast said I will do for thee." And again Moses: "Show me thy glory." And the Lord likewise of the future: "I will go before in my glory," and the rest. And at the last: "And then thou shalt see my hinder parts." Not loins nor calves, but the glory which he had desired, to be revealed in later times. In which face, face to face visible, he had promised himself to him, saying to Aaron too, "And if there be a prophet among you, in a vision I will be known to him, and in a vision I will speak to him, not as to Moses: mouth to mouth I will speak to him in appearance" (surely of a man, which he was to bear), "not in a riddle." For even though Marcion was unwilling that he should be shown speaking with the Lord, but standing, yet even standing he stood mouth to mouth and face to face with him, "with him," it says, not outside him, into his glory, not to say in his sight. From which glory, illumined no otherwise, he departed from Christ than he was wont from the Creator — and so then to smite the eyes of the sons of Israel, just as now those of the blinded Marcion, who did not see that this argument too works against himself.

23. I take upon myself the person of Israel. Let the Christ of Marcion stand and cry out: "O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I bear with you?" Straightway he ought to hear from me: "Whoever thou art, thou newcomer, first publish who thou art, and from whom thou comest, and what right thou hast in us. Hitherto with thee all is the Creator's. Plainly if thou comest from him, and for him thou actest, we admit the reproach. But if from another, say, I pray, what hast thou ever committed to us of thine own, which we ought to have believed, that thou shouldst reproach unbelief — thou who hast never even revealed thyself to us? How long since didst thou begin to act among us, that thou shouldst complain of the time? In what didst thou bear with us, that thou shouldst impute patience? An ass from Aesop's well, thou comest only now, and already criest out." I take up also the person of the disciples, on whom he leapt: "O unbelieving nation, how long shall I be with you, how long shall I bear with you?" This outburst of his I should most justly strike back, surely in this manner: "Whoever thou art, thou newcomer, first publish who thou art, from whom thou comest, what right thou hast in us. Hitherto, I think, thou art the Creator's, and therefore we have followed thee, recognizing in thee all that is his. But if thou comest from him, we admit the reproach. But if for another thou actest, I pray thee, say, what hast thou ever committed to us, at least of thine own, which we ought already to have believed, that thou shouldst reproach unbelief — thou who dost not even hitherto publish thine author? How long since didst thou begin to act among us, that thou shouldst oppose the time too? In what didst thou bear with us, that thou shouldst boast patience too? An ass from Aesop's well, thou hast only now appeared here, and already criest out." Who would not so have beaten back the injustice of the reproach, if he had believed him to belong to one who ought not yet to complain? Save that not even that other would have leapt upon them, had he not, long since dwelling among them in the law, in the prophets, in powers and benefits, ever found them unbelieving. But behold, Christ loves the little ones, teaching that such ought they to be who always wish to be greater. But the Creator sent bears upon the boys, avenging Elisha the prophet, who had suffered insults from them. A shameless enough Antithesis, when it commits things so diverse — little ones and boys, an age yet innocent and one already capable of judgement, which could insult, not to say blaspheme. By which, then, as just god, he spared not even impious boys, exacting honour for the greater age, and surely the more from the lesser; but by which, as good, he so loves the little ones that in Egypt he did good to the midwives, who protected the Hebrew births endangered by the edict of Pharaoh. Thus this affection too of Christ is with the Creator. Even now, the god of Marcion, who opposes marriage, how can he seem a lover of little ones, whose whole cause is marriage? He who hates the seed must of necessity execrate the fruit too. Nay, that one is to be held more savage than the king of Egypt. For Pharaoh did not suffer the infants to be reared, this one not even to be born — taking life from them even of ten months in the womb. But how much more credible that the affection toward little ones be reckoned to him who, in blessing marriage for the propagation of the human race, blessed and promised the very fruit of marriage, of which infancy is the first part. The Creator represents a plague of fire at Elias' demand upon that false prophet. I acknowledge the severity of a judge. On the contrary, the disciples destining the same animadversion against Christ upon that little village of the Samaritans. Let the heretic acknowledge too that this gentleness of Christ was promised by the same most severe judge. "He shall not contend," it says, "nor shall his voice be heard in the street: the bruised reed he shall not break, and the smoking flax he shall not quench." Such a one, surely, was much more not about to burn men. For then too to Elias, "Not in fire," says the Lord, "but in a mild spirit." But why does the most humane god refuse him who offers himself so inseparable a companion to him? If because he had said proudly or out of hypocrisy, "I will follow thee wherever thou goest," then either pride or hypocrisy he acted as a judge in judging it to be refused. And surely he condemned whom he refused, namely not about to follow unto salvation. For as he calls to salvation whom he does not refuse, or even whom he calls spontaneously, so to perdition he condemns whom he refuses. But to that man pleading the burial of his father, when he answers, "Let the dead bury their dead, but go thou and announce the kingdom of God," he manifestly confirmed both laws of the Creator: both that in Leviticus, forbidding the priests to be present even at the last rites of parents ("Over every dead soul," it says, "the priest shall not enter, and over his own father he shall not be defiled"), and that of consecration in Numbers; for there too he who vows himself to God bids, among the rest, that he enter not over any dead soul, not even over a father's or mother's or brother's. But I think he was destining for both consecration and priesthood him whom he had imbued with preaching the kingdom of God. Or if it is not so, he must be pronounced impious enough who, with no reason of law intervening, commanded the burials of parents to be despised by their sons. But when he forbids that third one, preparing first to bid farewell to his own, to look back, he follows out the sect of the Creator. This too that other one had been unwilling to have done by those whom he had freed from Sodom.

24. He chooses too another seventy apostles over and above the twelve. For to what end twelve, after just so many springs in Elim, if not also seventy after just so many palm-trees? The diversity of cases, not of powers, made most of the Antitheses. But he who did not regard the diversity of cases, easily esteemed it one of powers. The Creator brings out the departure of the sons of Israel from Egypt, stuffed and packed with those spoils of golden and silver vessels and garments besides the burdens of their dough; but Christ prescribed that the disciples should not carry even a staff on the way. For the former were being advanced into the wilderness, but these were sent into cities. Consider the bringing-forward of the cases, and you will understand one and the same power which arranged the expedition of its own according to penury and plenty — cutting short, as it was to abound through the cities, just as it had provided furnishing for one about to journey through the wilderness. He forbade them also to carry shoes. For he it was under whom the people, even in the wilderness through so many years, had not worn out its shoes. "Salute no one," he says, "on the way." O Christ the destroyer of the prophets, from whom he received even this! Elisha, when he sent his servant Gehazi on the way to the son of the Shunammite, to be raised from death, I think thus commanded him: "Gird thy loins and take my staff in thy hand and go: whomever thou meetest on the way, do not bless him" — that is, do not salute him — "and whoever blesses thee, do not answer him" — that is, do not salute him back. For what is the blessing on the ways but a mutual salutation from meeting? So too the Lord, that into whatever house they should enter, they should say peace to it. The example is the same. For this too Elisha commanded — that, when he had entered to the Shunammite, he should say to her, "Peace to thy husband, peace to thy son." These will rather be our Antitheses, which compare, not which separate Christ. But "the worker is worthy of his hire" — who could more have pronounced this than a god a judge? — for this very thing is to judge, to make the worker worthy of his hire. No retribution stands without judgement. Even now here the law of the Creator is sealed, who judges even the working oxen worthy workers of their hire. "An ox," it says, "treading out, thou shalt not bind the mouth." Who so generous toward men but he who is so toward cattle too? But if Christ too pronounces the workers worthy of their hire, he excused that precept of the Creator about the golden and silver vessels of the Egyptians to be carried off. For those who had worked villas and cities for the Egyptians, surely workers worthy of their hire, were not equipped for fraud, but for the compensation of a hire which otherwise they could not have exacted from their masters. The kingdom of God, neither new nor unheard-of, he thus too confirmed, while he bids it be announced to have drawn near. For what at some time had been far off, that can be said to have drawn near. But if it had never before existed before it drew near, neither could that be said to have drawn near which had never been far off. Everything that is new and unknown is sudden. Everything that is sudden, when it is announced, then for the first time, bringing in its appearance, then for the first time receives its time. For the rest, it could not have delayed before, so long as it was not announced, nor have drawn near from the time it began to be announced. He even adds, that to those who had not received them they should say, "Know, however, that the kingdom of God has drawn near." If he commands this not for the sake of threatening too, he commands it most vainly. For what is it to them if the kingdom draw near, except because it draws near with judgement? — unto the salvation, namely, of those who shall have received its announcement. How, if a threat can be without execution, have you a god an executor in the threatener and a judge in both? So too he bids the dust be shaken off upon them, for a testification, even what cleaves to their land — far less anything of the remaining communion. For if inhumanity and inhospitality are to bring back from him no vengeance, to what purpose does he prefix a testification, surely portending threats? Now, since the Creator too in Deuteronomy forbids the Ammonites and Moabites to be received into the church, because they had inhumanly and inhospitably defrauded of supplies the people departing from Egypt, then it will be established that the interdict of communion flowed thence into Christ, where he has the form, "Whoever despises you, despises me." This too the Creator to Moses: "They have not despised thee, but me." For Moses is as much an apostle as the prophets too are apostles. The authority of either office will have to be matched, from one and the same lord of apostles and of prophets. Who now will give power to tread upon serpents and scorpions? Whether the lord of all animals, or the god not even of one lizard? But well that the Creator promised this power even to little boys through Isaiah — to thrust their hand into the den of asps and into the bed of the young of asps, and not at all be hurt. And surely we know (saving the simplicity of the Scripture — for not even could the beasts themselves harm where faith was) that figuratively scorpions and serpents portend spiritual things of wickedness, of which their very prince too is reckoned under the name of serpent and dragon and of each most eminent beast with the Creator, who granted this power to his former Christ, as the ninetieth psalm to him: "Upon the asp and the basilisk thou shalt tread, and thou shalt trample the lion and the dragon." As also Isaiah: "In that day the Lord God shall bring on a sword, holy, great, and strong" — namely his Christ — "upon that dragon, the great and crooked serpent, and he shall slay him in that day." But when the same says, "It shall be called a clean way and a holy way, and the unclean shall not pass there, nor shall there be there an unclean way; but those who shall be dispersed shall go in it, and shall not err, and there shall no longer be a lion there, nor shall any of the worst beasts go up upon it, nor shall it be found there" — since the way demonstrates faith, through which we come to God, even then to the same way, that is, to faith, he promises this evacuation and subjection of the beasts. In short, you may find too the times of the promise to agree, if you read what goes before: "Be strong, you hands let down, and you knees dissolved: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear: then the lame shall leap as a hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall be clear." Therefore where he published the benefits of medicines, then too he subjected both scorpions and serpents to his holy ones — he, namely, who had received this power, that he might furnish it to others too, first from the Father, and exhibited it according to the order of the proclamation.

25. Who shall be invoked as Lord of heaven who is not first shown to be its maker? "For I give thanks," he says, "and confess to thee, Lord of heaven, that what was hidden from the wise and prudent thou hast revealed to babes." What things are these? and whose? and by whom hidden? and by whom revealed? If hidden by the god of Marcion and revealed, who had sent forth absolutely nothing before in which anything could have been hidden — no prophecies, no parables, no visions, no arguments at all of things or words or names overshadowed through allegories and figures or the mists of riddles, but had hidden his very magnitude, which he was now most of all revealing through Christ — unjustly enough. For what had the wise and prudent delinquished, that god should be hidden from them, to the knowing of whom their wisdom and prudence had not sufficed? No way being given by him through any proclamation of works, or any footprints, by which the wise and prudent might be led on. Although too even if they had delinquished in something toward an unknown god — suppose now a known one — yet they ought not to have experienced him a jealous one, who is brought in as unlike the Creator. Therefore if he had neither sent forth materials in which to have hidden anything, nor had had guilty parties from whom to hide it, nor ought to have hidden it, even if he had had them — then neither will he himself be the revealer, who was not the hider; thus neither the Lord of heaven nor the Father of Christ, but he in whom all these things suit. For he both hid, the instrument of prophetic obscurity being sent before, whose understanding faith should deserve ("Unless you believe, you shall not understand"), and had as guilty the wise and prudent, who from his works so many and so great did not seek out an intelligible god, or philosophized perversely concerning him, and supplied wits to the heretics, and lastly is jealous. In short, of old he harangued through Isaiah what Christ rejoices at: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will hide." As also elsewhere he signifies both to have hidden and to be about to reveal: "And I will give them hidden treasures, the invisible I will open to them." And again: "Who else shall scatter the signs of ventriloquists and the divinations from the heart, turning back the wise and infatuating their thoughts?" But if he designated his own Christ too the illuminator of the nations — "I have set thee for a light of the nations," which we interpret in the name of the babes, namely those once small in sense and infants in imprudence, but now too small through the humility of faith — surely we shall the more easily believe that the same one revealed too to the babes through Christ who both formerly hid and through Christ promised the revelation. Or if the god of Marcion has laid open those things which had formerly been hidden by the Creator, then now he has done business for the Creator, expounding his things. "But for destruction," you say, "that he might traduce them." Then he ought to have traduced them to those from whom the Creator hid them — the wise and prudent. For if he did it out of benignity, acknowledgement was to be furnished to those to whom it had been denied, not to babes, to whom the Creator had begrudged nothing. And yet hitherto, I think, we prove that rather a building-up of the law and the prophets is found in Christ than a destruction. He says all things were handed over to him by the Father. You might believe it if Christ is the Creator's, whose all things are, because the Creator handed over all things to a Son not lesser than himself — the things he founded through him, namely through his Word. But if that newcomer is meant, what are the "all things" which were handed over to him by the Father? Which are the Creator's? Therefore good are the things which the Father handed to the Son, and the Creator now good, whose all things are good, and that other now not good, who invaded another's goods, that he might hand them to a Son, teaching to abstain from another's. Certainly a most beggarly one, who had not whence to enrich even his Son but out of another's. Or if nothing of the Creator's was handed to him by the Father, how does he claim the Creator's man for himself? Or if the man alone was handed to him, "all things" is not the man. But the Scripture declares a handing over of all things made to the Son. But even if you interpret "all things" of the kinds of men, that is, of all the nations, even to have handed these over to the Son is the Creator's: "I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession." Or if that other too has some things of his own, all of which he handed to the Son, equally with the man of the Creator, show some one out of all for credence, for an example, lest I as deservedly not believe that all things are his of whom I see nothing, as deservedly believe even the things I do not see to be his whose are all the things I do see. "But no one knows who the Father is, save the Son, and who the Son is, save the Father, and to whomever the Son shall reveal him." And so Christ preached an unknown god. For hence too the other heretics are propped, opposing the Creator as known to all, both to Israel by familiarity and to the nations by nature. And how does he himself attest that he was not known even to Israel? "But Israel has not known me, and the people has not understood me"; nor to the nations: "For behold, of the nations," he says, "there is no one." Wherefore he reckoned them a drop of a bucket, and Zion he left as a watch-tower in a vineyard.
