See, then, whether it be a confirmation of the prophetic voice reproaching the merely human ignorance, which was up to the Son. For therefore he subjoined that the Father is known by him to whom the Son shall have revealed him, since he himself was the one who, set by the Father, was announced as the illumination of the nations — of God, namely, the nations to be illumined, even Israel — surely through a fuller acknowledgement of God. Thus the arguments will not avail for the faith of another god which can suit the Creator, because those which do not suit the Creator, these will be able to avail for the faith of another god. If you inspect what follows too — "Blessed are the eyes which see what you see: for I say to you, that prophets did not see what you see" — they descend from the higher sense, so that no one, as was fitting, had known God, since not even the prophets had seen what was being seen under Christ. For if Christ were not mine, he would not have placed mention of the prophets in this passage. For what wonder if they had not seen the things of an unknown god, and one revealed after so long an age? But what would have been the happiness of those who then saw what others could not with reason have seen, if they had not obtained the representation of those things which they had never proclaimed — except that those who could equally have seen the things of their own god, which they had even proclaimed, yet had not seen them? But this will be the happiness of others who saw what others had only proclaimed. In short, we will show — and have already shown — that the things were seen in Christ which had been proclaimed, yet hidden even from the prophets themselves, that they might be hidden too from the wise and prudent of the world. In the gospel of truth a doctor of the law, assailing the Lord, "What doing," he says, "shall I obtain eternal life?" In the heretical one, only "life" is set, without mention of "eternal," so that the doctor may seem to have consulted about that life which is promised in the law by the Creator as long-lasting, and the Lord therefore to have given him an answer according to the law, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart and with thy whole soul and with all thy strength," because it was about the law of life he was inquiring. But the doctor of the law surely knew by what manner he could obtain the legal life, so that he would not have asked about that whose rules he even taught. But because the dead too were now being raised by Christ, roused to the hope of eternal life through the examples of return, lest he should demand something more of observance, loftier in hope, he therefore consulted about the obtaining of eternal life. And so the Lord, as himself neither another, nor bringing in any new precept other than that which principally makes for all salvation and either life, sets the very head of the law against him — of loving in all ways the Lord his God. In short, if the doctor too consulted about long-lasting life, and Christ answered, which is with the Creator, not about eternal, which is with the god of Marcion, how does he obtain the eternal? Surely not in the same way as the long-lasting too. For according to a difference of rewards, a distance of works too must be believed. Therefore not out of love of your god will the Marcionite obtain eternal life, as the lover of the Creator the long-lasting. But what kind of thing is it that he should not the more be loved who promises the eternal, if he is to be loved who promises the long-lasting? Therefore both lives will belong to the same one, since the same discipline is to be caught at for either life. What the Creator teaches, that it needs Christ too to be loved that he may furnish — that objection too intervening here, by which the greater ought the more easily to be believed with him with whom the lesser go before, than with him for whom no lesser things prepared any faith concerning the greater. Let it now be his concern whether our people added "eternal." This is enough for me, that that Christ, the inviter to eternal, not to long, life, consulted about the long, which he was destroying, exhorted a man rather to the eternal, which he was bringing in. What, I ask you, would the Christ of the Creator have done, if he who had built up a man toward loving the Creator were not the Creator's? I believe he would have denied the Creator to be loved.

26. When in a certain place he had prayed to that higher Father, with eyes shameless enough and rash looking up to the heaven of the Creator — by whom, so harsh and savage, he could have been struck with hail and lightning, just as Jerusalem too could be fastened down by him — one of the disciples accosting him, "Lord," he says, "teach us to pray, as John too taught his disciples" — namely because he esteemed that another god should be prayed to otherwise. He who had presumed this, let him first prove another god published by Christ. For no one would have wished to know how to pray before he had learned whom he should pray to. Therefore if he had learned, prove it. If nowhere yet do you prove it, know that he asked of him a form of prayer toward the Creator, to whom the disciples of John too prayed. But because John too had brought in some new order of prayer, therefore his disciple had not without reason presumed that this too should be demanded of Christ — that they too, after the proper institution of their own master, should pray, not another, but otherwise, to God; accordingly neither would Christ have conferred the knowledge of prayer on a disciple before that of the god himself. Thus he himself too taught prayer toward him whom the disciple hitherto had known. In short, recognize what god the sense of the prayer savours. To whom shall I say, "Father"? to him who did not make me at all, from whom I draw no origin, or to him who by making and instructing me begat me? From whom shall I ask the Holy Spirit? from whom not even the worldly spirit is furnished, or from whom even the angels are made spirits, whose spirit too in the beginning was borne over the waters? Whose kingdom shall I wish to come — whom I never heard king of glory, or in whose hand are even the hearts of kings? Who shall give me daily bread? — he who founds me not even a millet-grain, or he who furnished even from heaven the daily bread of angels to his people? Who shall remit my delinquencies? — he who by not judging them does not retain them, or he who, if he shall not remit them, will retain them, that he may judge? Who shall not suffer us to be led into temptation? — whom shall the tempter be able not to fear, or he who from the beginning pre-condemned the tempting angel? In this order, he who supplicates another god and not the Creator does not pray him, but defames him. Accordingly, from whom shall I ask, that I may receive? with whom seek, that I may find? at whom knock, that it may be opened to me? Who has it to give to the asker, save he whose all things are, whose even I am who ask? But what have I lost with that other god, that with him I should seek and find? If wisdom and prudence, the Creator hid these. With him, then, shall I seek? If salvation and life, these too with the Creator? Nothing shall be sought elsewhere to be found than where it lay hidden to appear. So neither shall I knock elsewhere than whence I have departed. In short, if to receive and to find and to be admitted is the fruit of labour and instance to him who asked and sought and knocked, understand that these things are commanded and promised by the Creator. For that best god, coming spontaneously to furnish to a man not his own, would have indicted no labour nor instance on him. For he would now be no longer best, if he did not spontaneously give to one not asking, and furnish finding to one not seeking, and open to one not knocking. But the Creator could indict these things through Christ, that, because by delinquency man had offended his god, he should labour and by instance of asking receive, and by seeking find, and by knocking enter in. So too the foregoing likeness makes the nocturnal asker of bread a friend, not a stranger, and one knocking at a friend's, not a stranger's. But a friend, even if he has offended, is rather the Creator's man than the god of Marcion's. And so he knocks at him to whom he had a right, whose door he knew, whom he knew to have loaves, lying now with his infants, whom he had willed to be born. Even that he is knocked at late is the Creator's time. His too is the late, whose is the age and the setting of the age. But at a new god no one would have knocked late, only just as he was dawning. It is the Creator who both shut the door once to the nations, which was once knocked at by the Jews; he both rises and gives, and, even if now not as to a friend, yet not as to a stranger man, but, as he says, as to a troublesome one. But so newly a god could suffer no one to be troublesome to him. Acknowledge therefore the Father too whom you even call Creator. He it is who knows what his sons ask. For to those asking bread from heaven he gave manna, and to those desiring flesh he sent forth the quail; not a serpent for a fish, nor a scorpion for an egg. But it will belong to him not to give evil for good whose both are. For the rest, the god of Marcion, not having a scorpion, could not say that he would not give what he did not have; but he who, having a scorpion too, does not give. And so the Holy Spirit too will be given by him with whom the not-holy too is. When he had cast out a deaf demon (that in this species of cure too he might meet Isaiah), said to cast out demons in Beelzebub, "If I," he says, "in Beelzebub cast out demons, in whom do your sons cast them out?" — by this voice what does he portend rather than that he casts out in him in whom their sons too do? In the power, namely, of the Creator. For if you think it is to be taken thus, "If I in Beelzebub, in whom your sons?" as though he were censuring them as casting out in Beelzebub, the former sense will resist you, that Satan cannot be divided against himself. So far neither did they cast out in Beelzebub, but, as we have said, in the power of the Creator, which, that he might make understood, he subjoins: "But if I in the finger of God expel demons, then has the kingdom of God drawn near unto you?" For with Pharaoh those sorcerers, employed against Moses, called the power of the Creator the finger of God. The finger of God is this, that it should signify even what is small, yet most strong. This too Christ showing — a reminder, not an obliterator, namely, of his own antiquities — called the power of God the finger of God, to be understood of none other than him with whom this had been so named. Therefore his kingdom too had drawn near whose power too was called a finger. With reason, then, he applied to the parable of that strong armed man, whom another stronger overpowered — the prince of demons, whom he had above called Beelzebub and Satan — signifying him overpowered by the finger of God, not the Creator subdued by another god. For the rest, how should his kingdom still stand within its boundaries and laws and offices, whom, though with the world entire, that stronger god of Marcion could even thus have seemed to overcome, if the Marcionites too did not even die according to his law, flowing down into the earth, often taught even by a scorpion that the Creator is not overcome? A woman out of the crowd cried out, "Blessed the womb that bore him, and the breasts that nourished him." And the Lord, "Nay, blessed are they who hear the word of God and do it." For before too he had thus rejected his mother or brothers, while he prefers the hearers and obeyers of God. For neither here did a mother stand by him. So far had he not before denied him born. When he hears this again, again accordingly he transferred the felicity from the womb and breasts of his mother to the disciples — from her from whom he would not have transferred it if he had her not.

27. Elsewhere I prefer to purge the things which the Marcionites reprehend in the Creator. For here it suffices if these are found in Christ. Behold, unequal himself, inconstant, light, teaching one thing, doing another; he bids give to everyone that asks, and himself gives no sign to those who ask. For so great an age he hid his light from men, and denies that a lamp is to be hidden away, but confirms that it is to be set forth upon a candlestick, that it may shine for all. He forbids to curse back, much more surely to curse, and drives in a "Woe" upon the Pharisees and doctors of the law. Who is so like my god's Christ as his own? Often already we have fixed it that he could in no way be noted a destroyer of the law if he had promulgated another god. And therefore then too the Pharisee, who had called him to dinner, debated within himself why he had not first washed before he reclined, according to the law — since he carried about the god of the law. But Jesus even interpreted the law for him, saying that they cleansed the outside of the cup and platter, but their own inward parts were full of rapine and iniquity — to signify that the cleanness of vessels was to be understood, with God, of men; because the Pharisee too had debated within himself about the man, not about the unwashed cup. Therefore, "You wash the outside," he says, "of the cup," that is, the flesh, "but your inward parts you cleanse not," that is, the soul; adding, "Is it not he who made the outside" — that is, the flesh — "who made the inward parts too" — that is, the soul? By which saying he openly demonstrated that the cleanness of the outer and inner man pertains to the same God, whose both are, who prefers mercy not only to the washing of the man, but even to sacrifice. For he subjoins, "Give what you have as alms, and all things shall be clean to you." But if another god too could have commanded mercy — yet not before he was known. And here too it appears that they were rebuked not concerning a god, but concerning his discipline, by whom both figuratively the cleansing of the vessels and manifestly the works of mercies were enjoined upon them. So too he chides those who tithe their little herbs but pass over the calling and the love of God. Of what god the calling and love, if not of him whose rue and mint too, after the form of the law, they offered out of tithes? For the whole of the reproach was this, that they cared for the modest things, surely toward him to whom they did not exhibit the greater things — to him who says, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with all thy strength," who called thee out of Egypt. For the rest, neither would the time have allowed that Christ should demand so precocious — nay, so unripe a love as yet — for a new and recent god, not to say one not yet made manifest. When he accuses too those who catch at the chief places and the honour of salutations, he administers the sect of the Creator, who calls such princes rulers of the Sodomites, who forbids even trust in superiors — nay, pronounces altogether most wretched the man who has hope in man. But if for this reason anyone affects a princedom, that he may glory in the offices of others, since he forbade offices of this kind of hoping and trusting in man, the same rebuked too the affecters of princedoms. He inveighs too against the doctors of the law themselves, that they loaded others with unbearable burdens, which they themselves dared not attempt even with a finger — not censuring the burdens of the law as if its detester. For how a detester, who, while he was most of all accusing those who passed over the more weighty things of the law — alms and the calling and the love of God — did not even hold these heavy, far less the tithes of rue and the cleanness of platters? For the rest, he would rather have judged them to be excused if they could not bear unbearable things. But what burdens does he tax? Those which they themselves heaped up out of their own, teaching precepts, the doctrines of men, for the cause of their own conveniences, joining house to house, that they might carry off what was their neighbours', crying down the people, loving gifts, following after retribution, plundering the things judged for the poor, that there might be to them the widow for spoil and the orphan for prey. Concerning whom the same Isaiah: "Woe to those who are strong in Jerusalem"; and again: "Those who demand of you, lord it over you." Who more than the doctors of the law? These, if they displeased Christ too, displeased as his own. For of an alien law he would not at all have assailed the doctors. But why do they hear a "Woe" too because they built monuments to the prophets slain by their fathers — they rather worthy of praise, who by that work of piety testified that they did not consent to the deeds of their fathers — if he were not a jealous one, such as the Marcionites arraign him, exacting the delinquencies of the fathers from the sons even to the fourth nativity? But what key had the doctors of the law except the interpretation of the law? to the understanding of which neither did they themselves approach, not believing, namely (for "Unless you believe, you shall not understand"), nor did they admit others, teaching rather precepts and the doctrines of men. He, then, who rebuked those who neither entered themselves nor furnished entry to others — is he to be held a disparager of the law or a fautor? If a disparager, then the closers of the law too ought to have pleased him; if a fautor, then he is no longer the rival of the law either. But all these things he drove in to blacken the Creator, as savage, toward whom delinquents should have a "Woe." And who would not rather fear to provoke a savage one by falling away from him? So much the more, then, he taught one to be deserved well of whom he drove in as one to be feared. So it behoved the Christ of the Creator.

28. With reason, therefore, the hypocrisy of the Pharisees did not please him — those, namely, who loved God with their lips, not with their heart. "Beware," he says to the disciples, "of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy" — not the preaching of the Creator. The Son hates those contumacious toward the Father; he does not wish his own to be such toward him, not toward another, toward whom hypocrisy might be committed, of which the example should be guarded against by the disciples. Thus he forbids the example of the Pharisees. He was forbidding it to be committed against him against whom the Pharisees committed it. Therefore, since he had taxed their hypocrisy — concealing the hidden things of the heart, namely, and overshadowing the secrets of unbelief with superficial offices, which, having the key of acknowledgement, neither entered itself nor suffered others — therefore he adds, "But nothing is covered which shall not be laid open, and nothing hidden which shall not be discerned"; lest anyone esteem that he intends the revelation and re-acknowledgement of a god formerly unknown and hidden, when he subjoins even the things which they muttered or treated among themselves — namely, saying about himself, "This man does not expel demons but in Beelzebub" — as about to proceed into the open, and to be in the mouth of men, from the promulgation of the gospel. Thereupon, turning to the disciples, "But I say to you, my friends," he says, "be not terrified by those who can only kill you, and after this have no further power over you." But to these Isaiah will be foretelling: "See how the just is taken away, and no one notices." "But I will show you whom you should fear: Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to send into Gehenna" — surely signifying the Creator: "Therefore, I say to you, fear him." And in this passage it would suffice me, if he whom he bids be feared he forbids to be offended, and whom he forbids to be offended he bids be deserved well of, and he who commands these things is his own to whom by fearing and not offending and deserving well of he procures it. But I have also to take from what follows. For "I say to you, everyone who shall confess in me before men, I too will confess in him before God." But those who shall confess in Christ shall have to be killed before men, surely about to suffer nothing more after the killing by them. These, then, will be those whom above he forewarns not to fear that they only be killed; therefore premising that the killing is not to be feared, that he might subjoin that the confession is to be sustained: "And everyone who shall deny me before men shall be denied before God" — by him, surely, who was to confess one confessing him. For if he shall confess the confessor, he himself it is who will also deny the denier. Now, if the confessor is one who has nothing to fear after the killing, the denier will be one who has to fear even after death. And so, since that which is to be feared after death is the Creator's — namely the penalty of Gehenna — then the denier too is the Creator's. But if the denier, then the confessor too, who after the killing is to suffer nothing from man, but plainly something from God if he denied. And thus Christ is the Creator's, who shows that his deniers ought to fear the Gehenna of the Creator. After the deterring of denial, therefore, follows too the admonition of a blasphemy to be dreaded: "He who shall speak against the Son of man, it shall be remitted to him, but he who shall speak against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be remitted to him." But if now both the remission and the retention of delinquency savour of a god a judge, his will be the Holy Spirit not to be blasphemed — not about to remit blasphemy, namely — just as above not to be denied — about to kill even into Gehenna, namely. But if Christ averts blasphemy too from the Creator, how he has come as his adversary I do not know. Or if by these things too he blackens his severity — not about to remit blasphemy and about to kill even into Gehenna — it remains that that diverse god's spirit too may be blasphemed with impunity, and that Christ may be denied, and that there be no difference about his worship or contempt; and, just as from contempt no penalty, so from worship no reward is to be hoped. Those brought before powers he forbids to think for the interrogation about an answer. "For the Holy Spirit," he says, "shall teach you in that very hour what you ought to speak." If an evidence of this kind is the Creator's, his too will be the precept whose the example went before. Balaam the prophet in Numbers, summoned by king Balak to curse Israel, with which he was entering battle, while he was being filled with the spirit, pronounced not the malediction to which he had come, but the benediction which the spirit suggested to him in that very hour — having professed before, among the king's messengers, and presently before the king himself, that he would pronounce what God should put in his mouth. These are the new doctrines of the new Christ, which of old the servants of the Creator initiated. Behold, a plainly diverse example of Moses and of Christ. Moses spontaneously intervenes among quarrelling brothers and rebukes the injurious one: "Why dost thou strike thy neighbour?" And he is rejected by him: "Who set thee a master or a judge over us?" But Christ, when he was asked by a certain man to settle between him and his brother concerning the dividing of an inheritance, denied his service, and that indeed to so honest a cause. Already then my Moses is better than your Christ, studying the peace of brothers, meeting injury. But indeed the Christ of a best and not a judging god says, "Who set me a judge over you?" He could find no other voice of excuse but that one with which a wicked man and impious brother had shaken off the asserter of probity and piety. In short, he approved the evil voice by using it, and the evil deed, by the declining of composing peace between brothers. Or did he perhaps take it ill that Moses had been put to flight by that saying, and therefore in the like cause of the brothers debating willed to have confounded them by the recollection of the same saying? Plainly so. For he himself it was then who had been in Moses, who had heard such things — the Spirit, namely, of the Creator. I think I have already sufficiently elsewhere shown that the glory of riches is condemned by our god, who pulls the very magnates down from their throne and lifts up the poor from the dung-heap. From him, then, will be the parable of the rich man flattering himself on the produce of his fields, to whom God says, "Fool, this night they shall demand back thy soul; but the things thou hast prepared, whose shall they be?" So too, in short, the king who gloried among the Persians over the storehouses and granaries of his delights heard ill through Isaiah.

29. Who would not wish us to take care for the soul about food and for the body about clothing, but he who provided these things for man beforehand, and who, furnishing them thence, with reason forbids care of them as a rival of his own liberality? — who both fitted the very substance of the soul as superior to food, and figured the very matter of the body as superior to a tunic; whose ravens too neither sow nor reap nor lay up in storehouses, and yet are fed by him; whose lilies and grass neither weave nor spin, and yet are clothed by him; whose Solomon too, most glorious, yet was adorned with no flowerlet more elaborate. For the rest, nothing is so abrupt as that one should furnish, and another bid the furnishing to be securely managed — and that indeed a disparager of him. In short, whether as a disparager of the Creator he will not have it thought of such frivolities, about which neither ravens nor lilies labour, subjected spontaneously, namely, by reason of their worthlessness — will presently appear. Meanwhile, why does he accuse them of small faith, that is, of what faith? Of that which they could not yet exhibit perfect to a god whom they were as yet, at the moment of his being revealed, just learning? or of that which by this very title they owed to the Creator — to believe, namely, that he furnishes these things spontaneously to the human race, and not to be anxious about them? For also, when he subjoins, "For these things do the nations of the world seek" — not believing, namely, in a god the founder and supplier of all — whom he wished not to be like the Gentiles, those he reproached of small faith toward the same god toward whom he marked the Gentiles unbelieving. For the rest, when he adds too, "But your Father knows that you have need of these things," first I will ask whom Christ wishes to be understood as Father. If he demonstrates their Creator, he confirms him good too, who knows what his sons need; but if that other god, how does he know food and clothing to be necessary to man, of whom he furnished none? For if he had known, he would have furnished. For the rest, if he knows what is necessary to man, and yet did not furnish, it was either from malignity or from infirmity that he did not furnish. But by professing these things necessary to man, surely he confirmed them good. For nothing evil is necessary. And he will now no longer be a depreciator of the works and indulgences of the Creator — so that I may discharge what I deferred above. Now if another both foresaw and furnishes the things which he knows necessary to man, how does he himself promise them? Or is he good out of another's goods? "For seek," he says, "the kingdom of God, and these things shall be added to you." Surely by himself. But if by himself, what kind of one is he who shall furnish another's goods? If by the Creator, whose they are too, who is it that promises another's? If they accrue to the kingdom, to be restored in the second degree, his is the second degree whose is the first too, his food and clothing whose the kingdom too is. Thus the whole promise is the Creator's — the state of the parables, the levelling of the likenesses, if they look to no other than him to whom they have through all things matched. We are servants, for we have for lord the god. We ought to gird our loins, that is, to be expedited from the impediments of an entangled and complicated life. Likewise to have lamps burning, that is, minds kindled from faith and shining with the works of truth, and so to await the lord, that is, Christ. Returning whence? If from a wedding, it is the Creator's, whose the wedding is; if not the Creator's, neither would Marcion himself, invited to the wedding, have gone, regarding his god as a detester of weddings. The parable, then, would have failed in the person of the lord, if there were not one to whom weddings suit. In the following parable too he errs enough who arranges that thief, whose hour if the householder knew, he would not suffer his house to be undermined, into the person of the Creator. For how can the Creator seem a thief, lord of the whole man? No one steals or undermines his own goods, but rather he who descends into another's, and estranges the man from his lord. Now since he demonstrates the devil to us as the thief — whose hour too, had man known in the beginning, he would never have been undermined by him — therefore he bids that we be prepared, because at what hour we do not think the Son of man shall come, not as though he himself were a thief, but as the judge, namely, of those who shall not have prepared themselves, nor guarded against the thief. Therefore, if he himself is the Son of man, I hold the judge, and in the judge I defend the Creator; but if in the name of Son of man in this place he shows the Christ of the Creator, that he may portend him a thief whose coming we know not when — you have above the prescription that no one is a thief of his own goods, with that too safe, that in so far as he drives in the Creator to be feared, in so far doing his business he is the Creator's. And so, to Peter asking whether he had told the parable against them or against all, against them and against all who should preside over the churches he sets forth a likeness of stewards, of whom he who shall well have treated his fellow-servants, the lord being absent, shall, on his return, be set over all his goods; but he who shall act otherwise, the lord returning on the day he thought not, at the hour he knew not — namely that Son of man, the Christ of the Creator, not a thief, but a judge — shall be set apart, and his part shall be placed with the unbelievers. Accordingly, then, either here too he opposes a lord a judge and catechizes them toward him, or, if a best god, then he affirms even him a judge, though the heretic be unwilling. For they attempt to temper this sense, when it is claimed for his god. As though it were a thing of tranquillity and mildness only to set apart and to place his part with the unbelievers — as if he were not summoned, so as to be restored to his own state. As if this very thing were not done by judgement. Folly! What will be the issue of the set-apart? Surely the loss of salvation? — seeing that they shall be set apart from those who shall obtain salvation. What, then, the state of the unbelievers? Surely condemnation? Or if the set-apart and the unbelievers shall suffer nothing, equally on the other side the retained and the faithful shall obtain nothing. But if the retained and the faithful shall obtain salvation, the set-apart and the unbelievers must of necessity lose it on the other side. This will be judgement, which he who intends is the Creator's. What other shall I understand cutting the servants with few or many stripes, and according as each has committed against them, so exacting too of them, but a god a recompenser? Whom does it befit me to obey but a remunerator? Your Christ proclaims, "I have come to send fire upon the earth." That best one, lord of no Gehenna, who a little before had coerced the disciples, lest they should demand fire upon a most inhuman little village — when this one burnt up Sodom and Gomorrah with a fiery storm, when it was sung, "Fire shall go forth before him and shall consume his enemies," when too through Hosea he threatened, "I will send fire upon the cities of Judea," or through Isaiah, "A fire is kindled out of my indignation." Let him not lie. If he is not he who sent forth his voice even from the burning bush, let it be his to see what fire he contends is to be understood. Even if it is a figure, by this very thing, that he takes arguments for his sense from my element, he is mine who uses my things. His will be the likeness of the fire whose is the truth too. He himself will better interpret the quality of that fire, adding, "Do you think I have come to send peace upon the earth? No, I say to you, but separation." Indeed "a sword" is written. But Marcion emends it; as though separation too were not the work of a sword. Therefore he intends a fire too of subversion, who has denied peace. As the battle, such too the burning. As the sword, such too the flame, neither suiting the lord. In short, "There shall be divided," he says, "father against son, and son against father, and mother against daughter, and daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and mother-in-law against daughter-in-law." If this battle among parents was sung in the very words by the trumpet of the prophet, I fear lest Micah foretold it to the Christ of Marcion. And therefore he pronounced them hypocrites, who indeed approved the face of heaven and earth, but did not discern that time, namely, in which, fulfilling all the things which had been foretold concerning him, and teaching not otherwise, he ought to have been acknowledged. For the rest, who could know the times of him for whom he had nothing by which he might prove them? With reason he reproaches too that they did not judge what is just out of themselves. Of old he commands this through Zechariah: "Judge a just judgement and one of peace"; through Jeremiah: "Do judgement and justice"; through Isaiah: "Judge the orphan and justify the widow" — imputing too to the vineyard Sorek that it had made not judgement but an outcry. He, then, who had taught them to do it by precept, demanded that they do it also by their own choice. He who had sown the precept urged also its overflow. But indeed how absurd that he should command to judge justly who was destroying the just god a judge! For even the judge who sends into prison nor brings out thence until even the last farthing be paid, in the person of the Creator they discuss under the name of disparagement. To which I must of necessity meet at the same step. For as often as the severity of the Creator is opposed, so often is Christ his to whom by fear he compels obedience.

30. The question again about a cure made on the sabbath, how did he discuss it? "Does not each of you on the sabbaths loose his ass or ox from the stall and lead it to drink?" Therefore, working according to the condition of the law, he confirmed the law, did not dissolve it — the law that bids no work be done except what shall be done for every soul; how much rather for a human one? Everywhere I am acknowledged to demand the congruence of the parables. "The kingdom of God," he says, "is like to a grain of mustard, which a man took and sowed in his garden." Who is to be understood in the person of the man? Surely Christ, because, though Marcion's, he is called the Son of man, who received from the Father the seed of the kingdom, namely the word of the gospel, and sowed it in his garden, surely in the world, say now in man. But since he said "in his garden," and yet the world is not his, nor man, but the Creator's, then he who sowed in his own is shown to be the Creator. Or if, to escape this snare, they shall turn the person of the man from Christ to the man receiving the seed of the kingdom and sowing it in the garden of his heart, not even this matter will suit any but the Creator. For what kind of thing is it that the kingdom of a most gentle god should be that which even the heat of judgement follows with a tearful austerity? But concerning the following likeness I fear, perhaps, lest it portend further the kingdom of God. For he compared it to leaven, not to unleavened bread, which is more familiar to the Creator. This conjecture too suits those who beg for arguments. And so I too will drive out vanity with vanity, saying that the leavening too suits the kingdom of the Creator, because after it the oven or furnace of Gehenna follows. How often besides does he show himself a judge, and in the judge the Creator? As often surely as he casts out and condemns by rejecting. As here too, "When the householder," he says, "shall have risen and shut the door" — surely for cutting off the iniquitous. To whom, knocking, he will answer, "I know not whence you are," and again, to those enumerating that they had eaten and drunk before him and that he had taught in their streets, he will add, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Where? outside, namely, where they shall be shut out, the door shut by him. Therefore there will be punishment whence comes the exclusion unto punishment, when they shall see the just entering into the kingdom of God, but themselves detained outside. By whom? If by the Creator, who then will be within receiving the just into the kingdom? The good god. What, then, is there for the Creator to do there, to detain outside unto punishment those whom his adversary shut out, to be received by himself, if at all, the more to his adversary's spite? But that other too, about to shut out the iniquitous, must surely either know that the Creator will detain them unto punishment, or not know. Therefore either they will be detained against his will, and he who detains is lesser than the other, yielding to him unwillingly; or, if he wills it so to be done, he himself judged it should so be done, and the author of the Creator's infamy will not himself be better than the Creator. If these things stand by no reasoning — that one be believed to punish, another to free — then to one will belong both the judgement and the kingdom, and, while both belong to one, he who also judges is the Creator's.

31. To a dinner or to a supper what kind of men does he bid be invited? Such as he had shown through Isaiah: "Break thy bread to the hungry, and the beggars, and those who are without a roof, bring into thy house" — those, namely, who could not requite the return of this humanity. If Christ forbids this to be caught at, promising it again at the resurrection, it is the Creator's form, who is not pleased with those who love gifts, who follow after retribution. The parable too of the inviter — to which party it the rather meets, weigh. "A certain man made a supper and invited many." Surely the preparation of the supper figures the fullness of eternal life. I say, first, that strangers and those connected by no right are not wont to be invited to a supper; certainly the domestic and familiar are more readily wont. It is the Creator's, then, to have invited those to whom belonged the invited — both through Adam, as men, and through the fathers, as Jews — not his to whom they belonged neither by nature nor by prerogative. Next, if he who prepared the supper sends to the guests, even thus the supper is the Creator's, who sent to admonish the guests, already invited before through the fathers, but to be admonished through the prophets — not he who sent no one to admonish, nor who did anything beforehand toward inviting, but himself descended suddenly, just as he became known, already inviting, just as he invited, already forcing them into the banquet, making the same hour of supping and of inviting to supper. The invited excuse themselves. If by another god, with reason, because suddenly invited; if not with reason, then not suddenly. But if not suddenly invited, then by the Creator, by whom of old; whose vocation, in short, they had declined, first saying to Aaron, "Make us gods to go before us"; and thereafter hearing with the ear and not hearing, namely the vocation of God, who most pertinently to this parable through Jeremiah, "Hear," he says, "my voice, and I will be to you a lord and you to me a people, and you shall walk in all my ways, whatsoever I shall command you." Behold the invitation of God. "And they heard not," it says, "and turned not their ear." Behold the refusal of the people. "But they went away in the things which they desired in their evil heart. I bought a field, and I bought you a yoke of oxen, and I married a wife." And further he drives in: "And I sent to you all my servants the prophets." This will be the Holy Spirit, the admonisher of the guests, by day and before light. "And my people heard not, and inclined not their ears, and hardened their neck." This, when it had been reported to the householder, then moved (well that he is moved too, for Marcion denies his god is moved, so this too is mine), he bids a gathering be made from the streets and lanes of the city. Let us see whether in that sense by which again through Jeremiah: "Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel? or a land left untilled?" — that is, "Have I not those whom I may choose, or whence I may choose? since my people said, We come not to thee." And so he sent to call others from the same city still. Then, the place abounding, he commanded a gathering too from the ways and hedges, that is, us now from the foreign nations — by that emulation, namely, by which in Deuteronomy: "I will turn my face away from them, and I will show what shall be to them in the last things" — that is, others to possess their place — "because they are a perverse generation, sons in whom there is no faith. They have provoked me to emulation with a no-god, and have moved me to anger with their idols; and I too will provoke them to emulation with a no-nation, with a foolish nation I will move them to anger" — namely with us, whose hope the Jews bear, of which the Lord denies they shall taste, Zion being forsaken, like a watch-tower in a vineyard and a hut in a cucumber-field, after they refused even the last invitation in Christ. What out of this order, to be recounted according to the arrangement and proclamations of the Creator, can suit him who has neither the order nor the arrangement for the conspiration of the parable, who did his whole work at once? Or what will be his first vocation, and what the admonition in the second act? — to invite both parties at once, from the city, from the hedges, against the mirror of the parable. Nor can he now judge as disdainful those whom he never before invited, whom he most of all accosts at the moment. Or if he judges them, as for the future, about to despise the vocation, then for the future too he portends a gathering in their place from the nations. Plainly for this he is to come a second time, to preach to the nations. And if he is to come — yet, I think, not as if to invite the guests still, but already to place them. Meanwhile, you who interpret the vocation of this supper into a heavenly banquet of spiritual fullness and joyfulness, remember that the earthly promises too of wine and oil and corn and the very city are equally figured by the Creator as spiritual.

32. Who seeks the lost sheep and the lost drachma but he who lost it? Who lost it but he who had it? Who had it but he whose it was? If, then, the man is the thing of no other than the Creator, he had him whose he was, he lost what he had, he sought what he lost, he found who sought, he exulted who found. Thus the argument of either parable is void in regard to him whose neither the sheep nor the drachma is, that is, man. For neither did he lose, because he did not have; nor seek, because he did not lose; nor find, because he did not seek; nor exult, because he did not find. And so it is his to exult over the penitence of a sinner — that is, over the recovery of the lost — who professed of old that he preferred the penitence of the sinner to his death.

33. Whom two masters one cannot serve, because the one must of necessity be offended and the other defended, he himself declares, setting forth God and mammon. Then, whom he would have mammon understood to be, if you have no interpreter, you can learn from himself. For admonishing us, concerning worldly things, to provide for ourselves the supports of friendships, after the example of that servant who, removed from his office, relieves his master's debtors by diminishing their bonds, for a help to himself, "And I," he says, "say to you, make for yourselves friends out of the mammon of injustice" — out of money, namely, like that servant. For we all know money to be the author and lord of all the world's injustice. Seeing the cupidity of the Pharisees enslaved to it, he loosed off this opinion: "You cannot serve God and mammon." In short, the Pharisees, greedy of money, derided him, because they understood, namely, mammon said of money. Lest anyone esteem that in mammon the Creator is to be understood, and that Christ called them back from the servitude of the Creator — what? rather from this learn one god shown by Christ. For he named two masters, God and mammon, the Creator and money. In short, "You cannot serve God" — surely him whom they seemed to serve — "and mammon" — to whom they were rather destined. But if he were himself acting as another, he would have demonstrated not two masters but three. For the Creator too is a master, because he is a god, and surely the more a master than mammon, and the more to be regarded, as the more a master. For what kind of thing is it that he who had called mammon a master, and had joined it with God, should be silent about their true master, that is, the Creator? Or did he by being silent concede that he is to be served, if he denied only that himself and mammon could be served? Thus, when he sets one god — about to name the Creator too, if he himself were another — he named the Creator, whom without another god he did not set as master. And so this too will shine out, how it was said, "If in unjust mammon you have not been faithful, what is true who will entrust to you?" — in money, namely, unjustly, not in the Creator, whom even Marcion makes just. "And if in another's you have not been found faithful, mine who will give to you?" For what is unjust ought to be alien to the servants of God. But how was the Creator alien to the Pharisees, the proper god of the Jewish nation? If, then, these things fall not upon the Creator but upon mammon, "Who will believe to you what is truer?" and "Who will give you what is mine?" cannot have been said as by another concerning the grace of another god. For then he would seem to have so said, if, marking them unbelievers toward the Creator, not toward mammon, he had through the mention of the Creator made distinctions of another god, not about to commit his own truth to the unbelievers of the Creator. How then can he be seen as another, if he be not set forth for this, that he be separated from the matter in hand? But if the Pharisees too, justifying themselves before men, were placing the hope of reward in man, he rebuked them in that sense in which the prophet Jeremiah too: "Wretched the man who has hope in man." If he adds too, "But God knows your hearts," he was commemorating the force of that god who pronounced himself a lamp, searching the reins and hearts. If he touches pride, "What is exalted among men is detestable to God," he sets Isaiah before the eyes: "For the day of the Lord of Sabaoth is upon every contumelious and proud one, upon every lofty and exalted one, and they shall be humbled." I can now gather why for so great an age the god of Marcion was in hiding. He was waiting, I suppose, until he should learn all these things from the Creator. He learned, then, up to the times of John, and so thereafter proceeded to announce the kingdom of God, saying, "The law and the prophets unto John, from whom the kingdom of God is announced." As though we too do not acknowledge a certain boundary, John, set between the old and the new, at whom Judaism should cease and from whom Christianity should begin — yet not so that the settling of the law and the prophets and the initiation of the gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, Christ himself, should have been made by another power. For even if we have proved both that the old things were proclaimed to pass and the new to succeed by the Creator, if John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord about to bring on the gospel and promulgate the kingdom of God — even from this, that John came, he himself will be the Christ who was to follow John as forerunner; and if the old things ceased and the new began, John intervening, it will be no wonder that this is from the arrangement of the Creator — so that it may be the more proved whence soever than from the setting of the law and prophets at John, and from there the rising of the kingdom of God. Let heaven and earth pass, then, sooner, just as the law and the prophets, than one apex of the words of the Lord. For "the word," says Isaiah, "of our God abides for ever." For since in Isaiah even then Christ — the Word, namely, and the Spirit of the Creator — had proclaimed John, the voice of one crying in the wilderness, "Prepare the way of the Lord" — for this, that he should come that the order of the law and prophets should thenceforth cease, through fulfilment, not through destruction, and that the kingdom of God should be announced by Christ — therefore he subjoined that the elements should sooner pass than his words, confirming this too, that what he had said of John had not passed away.

34. But Christ forbids divorce, saying, "He who shall dismiss his wife and shall marry another, commits adultery; he who shall marry one dismissed by a husband, is equally an adulterer." That even thus he may forbid divorce, he makes the marriage of a repudiated woman unlawful. But Moses permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: "If anyone take a wife and dwell with her, and it come to pass that she find no grace with him, because something unseemly is found in her, he shall write a bill of repudiation and shall give it into her hand, and shall dismiss her from his house." You see a diversity of law and gospel, of Moses and Christ? Plainly. For you have not received that other gospel too, of the same truth and the same Christ, in which, forbidding divorce, he solves the proper question of it: "Moses, for the hardness of your heart, commanded to give a bill of repudiation; but from the beginning it was not so" — because, namely, he who made male and female had said, "They shall be two in one flesh: what therefore God has joined, let not man put asunder." For by this answer he both protected the constitution of Moses, as his own, and directed the institution of the Creator, as Christ his own. But inasmuch as you must be refuted from those things which you have received, so I will meet you as though my Christ. Does not he too, while he forbids divorce, yet, bearing as Father him who joined male and female, rather excuse than destroy the constitution of Moses? But behold, suppose this Christ of yours be teaching contrary to Moses and the Creator, so that, if I shall not show it not contrary, he is mine. For I say that he now made a prohibition of divorce conditionally — if anyone for this reason dismiss his wife, that he may marry another. "He who shall dismiss," he says, "his wife, and shall marry another, has committed adultery; and he who shall marry one dismissed by a husband, is equally an adulterer" — one dismissed, surely, from the same cause from which it is not lawful to be dismissed, that another may be married; for he who marries one unlawfully dismissed, as though undismissed, is an adulterer. For the marriage abides which has not been rightly dissolved; the marriage abiding, to marry is adultery. Thus if he conditionally forbade dismissing a wife, he did not forbid it altogether; and what he did not forbid altogether, he permitted in other cases, where the cause ceases on account of which he forbade it. He even teaches nothing contrary to Moses, whose precept he somewhere preserves — not yet, I say, confirms. Or if you altogether deny that divorce is permitted by Christ, how do you yourself dissolve marriages, neither joining male and female, nor admitting those elsewhere joined to the sacrament of baptism and the eucharist, unless they have conspired between themselves against the fruit of marriage, as against the Creator himself? Certainly, what does a husband do with you, if his wife shall commit adultery? Shall he keep her? But not even your apostle suffers the members of Christ to be joined to a harlot. And so justice of divorce has even Christ as its asserter. From this point too Moses is confirmed by him, forbidding repudiation under the same title under which Christ does, if something unseemly be found in the woman. For also in the gospel of Matthew, "He who shall dismiss," he says, "his wife, except for the cause of adultery, makes her commit adultery." He too is equally reckoned an adulterer who shall marry one dismissed by a husband. For the rest, save for the cause of adultery, not even the Creator puts asunder what he himself joined — Moses elsewhere constituting that he who by violence had made a marriage cannot dismiss his wife for all time. But if a marriage compelled by violence shall stand, how much more a voluntary one out of agreement? — just as by the authority of prophecy too, "The wife of thy youth thou shalt not dismiss." You have therefore Christ spontaneously entering everywhere upon the footsteps of the Creator, both in permitting repudiation and in forbidding it. You have him too, however he wishes to lie hid, the foreseer of marriages, which he wishes neither to be separated by forbidding repudiation, nor to be held with a stain by then permitting divorce. Blush, who do not join those whom your Christ too joined. Blush, who put asunder without that desert by which your Christ too willed it put asunder. Now I must also show whence the Lord deduced this opinion, or whither he directed it. For so it will more fully be established that he did not look toward the destroying of Moses through a sudden proposal interposed concerning repudiation — because it was not suddenly interposed, having its root from the same mention of John. For John, censuring Herod because, against the law, he had married the wife of his deceased brother, who had a daughter by her (the law not permitting this otherwise — nay, even commanding it — except when a brother had died childless, that seed should be raised up to him by his own brother and from his rib), had been cast into prison, and afterward also slain by the same Herod. Mention being made, then, of John, and surely of the issue of his end, the Lord shot the figure of unlawful marriages and of adultery against Herod, pronouncing him too an adulterer who should marry one dismissed by her husband — the more to load the impiety of Herod, who had married one dismissed from her husband no less by death than by repudiation, and that while a brother had a daughter by her, and even on that account unlawfully, by the instinct of lust, not of law, and therefore had slain too the prophet, the asserter of the law. This to have discussed will profit me also toward the following argument of the rich man grieving in the underworld and the poor man resting in the bosom of Abraham. For that too, as to the surface of the Scripture, is suddenly set forth; as to the intention of the sense, this too coheres to the mention of John ill treated and of Herod ill married, deforming the issue of each — Herod's torments and John's refreshings — so that Herod might now hear, "They have there Moses and the prophets, let them hear them." But Marcion forces it elsewhere — namely, that he may determine that both rewards of the Creator, whether of torment or of refreshment, are placed in the underworld for those who shall have obeyed the law and the prophets, but may define that the bosom and harbour of Christ and his god is heavenly. We will answer to these things, the very Scripture refuting his eyes, which distinguishes the bosom of Abraham from the underworld for the poor man. For one thing, as I think, is the underworld, another too the bosom of Abraham. For he says that a great deep intervenes between those regions and prohibits passage from either side. But neither would the rich man have lifted up his eyes, and that from afar, but into the higher region, and from the distance of a height, through that immense interval of loftiness and of depth. Whence it appears to any wise man, who has at some time heard of the Elysian fields, that there is some local determination, which has been called the bosom of Abraham, for receiving the souls of his sons, even from the nations — of him, namely, the father of many nations to be reckoned into the census of Abraham, and out of the same faith by which Abraham too believed God, under no yoke of the law nor in the sign of circumcision. This region, then, I call the bosom of Abraham, though not heavenly, yet loftier than the underworld, which shall meanwhile furnish refreshment to the souls of the just, until the consummation of things discharge the resurrection of all with the fullness of reward — then to appear by the heavenly promise, which Marcion claims for his own, as though not promulgated by the Creator. To which Christ builds his ascent into heaven, according to Amos, surely for his own, where is also the eternal place, of which Isaiah: "Who shall announce to you the eternal place," save, namely, Christ, walking in justice, speaking the right way, holding in hatred injustice and iniquity? But if an eternal place is promised, and an ascent into heaven is built by the Creator, promising too that the seed of Abraham should be as the stars of heaven, surely on account of a heavenly promise — that promise being safe, why should it not admit that the bosom of Abraham be called some temporal receptacle of faithful souls, in which already the image of the future is delineated, and a certain white preview of either judgement is foreseen? — admonishing you heretics too, while you are in life, that Moses and the prophets preach one god the Creator, and one Christ his, and that either judgement, of penalty and of eternal salvation, is placed with the one god who kills and makes alive. "Nay," he says, "the decree of our god from heaven bade not Moses and the prophets be heard, but Christ: hear him." With reason. For then the apostles had already sufficiently heard Moses and the prophets, who had followed Christ by believing Moses and the prophets. For neither would Peter have received to say, "Thou art the Christ," before he had heard and believed Moses and the prophets, by whom alone as yet Christ was announced. This faith of theirs, then, had deserved that it should be confirmed even by the heavenly voice, bidding him be heard whom they had acknowledged evangelizing peace, evangelizing good things, announcing the eternal place, building for them his ascent into heaven. But in the underworld it is said of those: "They have there Moses and the prophets, let them hear them" — those who did not believe, or who did not so at all believe, that after death there are torments of the pride of riches and of the glory of delights, announced by Moses and the prophets, but decreed by that god who deposes magnates from thrones, and lifts up the needy from dung-heaps. Thus, since on either side the diversity of the pronouncement suits the Creator, no distance of divinities is to be established, but of the very matters.

35. Turning in the same place to the disciples, he says "Woe" to the author of scandals — that it would have been better for him if he had not been born, or if a millstone fastened to his neck he had been thrown into the deep, than that he should scandalize one of those little ones, namely his disciples. Estimate what kind of punishment he threatens him. For no other shall avenge the scandal of his disciples. Acknowledge, therefore, both a judge, and one pronouncing with that affection concerning the care of his own with which the Creator too of old: "He who touches you touches as it were the pupil of my eye." The same sense is of the same one. He bids a sinning brother be corrected; and he who shall not do this surely delinquishes, either out of hatred wishing his brother to persevere in his delinquency, or out of acceptance of persons sparing him — having Leviticus: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy mind; with a traducing thou shalt traduce thy neighbour" — surely thy brother too — "and thou shalt not take a delinquency on account of him." Nor is it wonderful if he so teaches who forbids you to despise even your brother's cattle, if you find them straying on the way, but to lead them back to your brother — far less the man himself to himself. But he bids you also give pardon to a brother delinquent against you, even seven times. Plainly little. For it is more with the Creator, who set no measure, pronouncing infinitely, "Be not mindful of thy brother's malice"; nor does he command that it be furnished to one asking, but even to one not asking. For he wishes the offence not to be forgiven but to be forgotten. Of how great interpretation the law of lepers is, touching the species of that very defect and the inspection of the high priest, is for us to know, for Marcion to oppose the tediousness of the law, that here too he may affirm Christ its rival, anticipating the solemnities of the law even in the cure of the ten lepers, whom, bidden only to go to show themselves to the priests, he cleansed on the way, without touch now and without a word, by a silent power and by his will alone — as though it were necessary, Christ being once announced the remedier of languors and defects and proved by his effects, that the qualities of the cures should be discussed, or that the Creator in Christ should be provoked to the law; if he did anything otherwise than the law distinguished, he himself perfected it, since surely the Lord works otherwise through himself or through his Son, otherwise through the prophets his servants — especially the evidences of his power and might, which, as clearer and stronger, since proper, it is right should differ from the vicarious. But of this kind things have already been said elsewhere in the former evidence. Now, even though he premised that there were then many lepers in Israel in the days of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian — surely the number too will not make for a difference of gods, toward the destruction of the Creator remedying one, and the preference of him who cleansed ten. For who will doubt that more could have been cured by him who had cured one, than by that one ten who had never before one? But by this pronouncement most of all he strikes the diffidence or pride of Israel, that, when there were many lepers there, and a prophet was not wanting, even when an evidence was put forth, no one ran to the god working in the prophets. Therefore, since he himself was the authentic pontiff of God the Father, he inspected them according to the secret of the law, signifying that Christ is the true discerner and disposer of human stains. But also what was in the manifest of the law he commanded, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." Why, if he was about to cleanse them before? Or as a mocker of the law, that, the cured being on the way, he might show that the law with its very priests was nothing? And let it surely be his concern, if to anyone Christ shall seem so opinionated. Nay, worthier things are to be interpreted, and juster as to faith. Therefore were they remedied, in that, bidden according to the law to go to the priests, they had obeyed; for it is not credible that observers of the law should have deserved medicine from a destroyer of the law. But why to the former leper did he command no such thing? Because neither did Elisha to Naaman the Syrian; and yet not on that account was he not the Creator's. I have answered enough; but he who has believed understands also something deeper. Learn, then, the causes too. The thing was being done in the regions of Samaria, whence too was meanwhile one of the lepers. But Samaria had revolted from Israel, having that schism out of the nine tribes, which, torn away through the prophet Ahijah, Jeroboam had placed at Samaria. But also otherwise the Samaritans were always self-pleasing concerning the mountains and wells of their fathers — as in the gospel of John that Samaritan woman in colloquy with the Lord at the well: "Art thou greater?" and the rest; and again: "Our fathers adored in this mountain, and you say that at Jerusalem one ought to adore." Therefore he who through Amos too had said "Woe" to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria, deigning now of set purpose to restore even her, bids them show themselves to the priests — surely who were nowhere but where the temple too was — subjecting the Samaritan to the Jew, since salvation is of the Jews, although both were Israelites and Samaritans. For the whole promise was Christ to the tribe of Judah; that they might know that at Jerusalem were both the priests and the temple and the mother of religion and the fountain, not the well, of salvation. And therefore, as he saw that they acknowledged the law to be discharged at Jerusalem, he remedied them, now to be justified out of faith without the order of the law. Whence too that one of the ten, loosed, mindful of the divine grace, the Samaritan whom he wonders at, he does not bid offer the gift out of the law, because he had already offered enough, rendering glory to God — this too at the Lord's wish, that the law might be interpreted. And yet to what god did the Samaritan render grace, when not even the Israelite had as yet learned of another god? To what other than him to whom all formerly remedied by Christ had? And therefore, "Thy faith has made thee safe," he heard, because he had understood that he ought to make a true oblation, namely the act of thanksgiving, to the omnipotent God, at the true temple and to his true high priest, Christ. But neither can the Pharisees seem to have consulted the Lord about the kingdom of another god, when it would come, so long as no god other than Christ had been published, nor he to have answered about another's kingdom than about whose he was consulted. "The kingdom of God comes not with observation," he says, "nor do they say, Behold here, behold there: for behold, the kingdom of God is within you." Who will not so interpret it: "Within you is," that is, in your hand, in your power, if you hear, if you do the precept of God? But if the kingdom of God is in the precept, then set against it, according to our antitheses, Moses, and it is one opinion. "The precept," he says, "is not lofty, nor far from thee. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldst say, Who shall ascend into heaven and bring it down to us, and we shall hear it and do it? Nor is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldst say, Who shall cross over and take it for us, and we shall hear it and do it? The word is near thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, and in thy hands to do it." This will be, "Not here, nor there; for behold, the kingdom of God is within you." And lest heretical audacity argue that the Lord answered them about the kingdom of the Creator, concerning which he was consulted, not about his own, the sequel resists. For saying that the Son of man must first suffer many things and be reprobated, before his coming, in which the kingdom too shall be substantially revealed, he showed his own the kingdom too concerning which he had answered, which was awaiting his passions and reprobations. But being about to be reprobated, and afterward acknowledged and assumed and exalted, he plucked the very word "reprobated" thence where, in the riddle of the stone, either revelation of him was sung with David — the first refusable, the second honourable. "The stone," it says, "which the builders reprobated, the same is made into the head of the corner. By the Lord was this done." For it is idle, if we have believed God to have proclaimed concerning the contumely or glory, namely, of someone, that he should not portend him whom he had portended both in the figure of a stone and of a rock and of a mountain. But if he speaks of his own coming, why does he compare it to the days of Noah and of Lot, foul and atrocious — a god gentle and mild? Why does he admonish to remember the wife of Lot, who contemned the precept of the Creator not with impunity, if he does not come with judgement to avenge his own precepts? Even if he avenges as that one, if he judges me, he ought not to have formed me by the evidences of him whom he destroys, lest that one seem to form me. But if here too he speaks not of his own coming, but of the Jews' Christ, let us await even now lest he proclaim anything of his own, believing meanwhile him to be the one whom in every place he proclaims.

36. For commanding too the perseverance and instance of praying, he sets forth the parable of the judge compelled to hear the widow by the instance and perseverance of her interpellations. Therefore he shows that a god a judge is to be prayed, not himself, if he himself is not the judge. But he subjoined that God would make the vengeance of his elect. If, then, he himself shall be the judge who is also the avenger, he has therefore proved the Creator the better god, whom he shows the avenger of his elect crying to him day and night. And yet, when he brings in the temple of the Creator, and describes two adoring with diverse mind — the Pharisee in pride, the publican in humility — and therefore the one reprobated, the other justified to have gone down — surely, by teaching by what discipline he is to be prayed, he constitutes him also to be prayed here from whom they were to bring back that discipline of praying, whether the reprobatrix of pride or the justificatrix of humility. Of another god I find with Christ neither temple nor worshippers nor judgement, but the Creator's. Him he bids be adored in humility, as the lifter-up of the lowly, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. What other to be adored has he shown me? by what discipline? by what hope? None, I think. For even the prayer which he taught we have proved to suit the Creator. It is another matter if he, as a best and spontaneously good god, does not even wish to be adored. But "Who is good, except one God only?" he says. Not as though out of two gods he had shown one to be best, but that one only is best, the only god, who is so the one best, because the only god. And surely best, who rains upon the just and unjust, and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing and helping even the Marcionites. In short, asked by a certain man, "Good master, what doing shall I possess eternal life?" he inquired about the precepts of the Creator, whether he knew them, that is, did them — to attest that everlasting life is acquired by the precepts of the Creator; and when that man had affirmed that he had observed from his youth all the more principal things, "One thing," he says, "is wanting to thee: all things whatsoever thou hast, sell, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me." Come now, Marcion, and all you fellow-sufferers and co-hateful ones of his, you heretics, what will you dare to say? Did Christ rescind the prior precepts, of not killing, of not committing adultery, of not stealing, of not testifying false, of loving father and mother? or did he both keep them and add what was lacking? Although this precept too of largesse to the needy is everywhere diffused in the law and the prophets, so that that most glorious observer of the precepts was traduced as about to hold his money far dearer. So this too is safe in the gospel: "I came not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfil." At the same time he freed too the rest from doubt, manifesting that the name both of God and of "good" is one, and eternal life, and treasure in heaven, and himself — whose precepts by supplying he both preserved and increased — to be recognized in this place too according to Micah, who says, "If it has been announced to thee, man, what is good, or what does the Lord require of thee, but to do judgement, to love mercy, and to be prepared to follow the Lord thy God?" For Christ too, a man, announcing what is good, the knowledge of the law, "The precepts," he says, "thou knowest." To do judgement: "Sell," he says, "what thou hast." To love mercy: "And give," he says, "to the needy." To be prepared to go with the Lord: "And come," he says, "follow me." So distinguished was the Jewish nation from the beginning by tribes and peoples and families and houses, that no one could easily be ignorant of his lineage, even from the recent Augustan censuses, then perhaps still pending. But the Jesus of Marcion (and one would not doubt born who appeared a man) surely, in that he was not born, could have had no public knowledge of his lineage, but was to be reckoned some one of those who in whatever way were held unknown. When, therefore, the blind man heard him passing by, why did he cry out, "Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me," unless because he was not rashly reckoned the son of David — that is, of the family of David — through his mother and brothers, who at some time, surely out of knowledge, had been announced to him? But those going before rebuked the blind man, that he should be silent — with reason, namely because he was crying out, not because he lied about the son of David. Or teach that those rebuking knew that Jesus was not the son of David, that on that account they may be believed to have enjoined silence on the blind man. But even if you should teach it, he would more easily presume them to be ignorant than that the Lord could have sustained a false proclamation about himself. But the Lord was patient. Yet not a confirmer of error — nay, even a detector of it — so that he would not have first cleared up this blindness of that man, lest he should further esteem Jesus the son of David. And yet, lest you should defame his patience, and affix to him any reason of dissimulation, and deny him the son of David — most manifestly he confirmed the blind man's proclamation both by the very reward of the medicine and by the testimony of his faith. "Thy faith," he says, "has made thee safe." What would you have the blind man have believed? That Jesus had come down from that god toward the casting-down of the Creator, toward the destruction of the law and the prophets? not that he was the one who was destined from the root of Jesse and from the fruit of the loins of David, the remunerator of the blind too? But not yet, I think, were the blind then such as Marcion is, that this should have been the faith of that blind man, by which he believed in the voice of "Jesus, son of David." He who both knew this of himself and willed himself to be known by all, gave the man's faith — even though better-eyed, even though sharer of the true light — an outer vision too, that we too might learn both the rule and at once the reward of faith. He who wishes to see Jesus the son of David, let him believe through the registration of the virgin. He who shall not so believe, shall not hear from him, "Thy faith has made thee safe," and so shall remain blind, rushing into the antithesis, the antithesis itself too rushing. For so the blind is wont to lead the blind. For if at some time the blind, in the recovery of Zion, had offended David, resisting that he should be admitted (into a figure of the people, accordingly blind, not about to admit one day Christ the son of David), therefore Christ on the contrary aided the blind man, that from this he might show himself not to be the son of David — that out of a diversity of mind he was good to the blind, whom that one had bidden be cut down. And why indeed did he say he had furnished it to a depraved faith? Nay, this too the son of David, the antithesis to be beaten back out of his own. For they too who had offended David were blind; but now a man of the same flesh had offered himself a suppliant to the son of David. Therefore, to him making satisfaction in a manner, the son of David, appeased, restored his sight, with the testimony of the faith by which he had believed this very thing, that the son of David was to be entreated by him. And yet David, I think, the audacity of men had offended, not their ill health.

37. There follows too the salvation of the house of Zacchaeus. By what desert? Had he too believed that Christ had come from Marcion? And yet there was still in the ears of all that voice of the blind man, "Have mercy on me, Jesus, son of David," and "All the people rendered praises to God" — not Marcion's, but David's. Truly Zacchaeus, even though a foreigner, perhaps yet, breathed upon by some knowledge of the Scriptures out of Jewish commerce — but it is more even if, ignorant of Isaiah, he had fulfilled his precepts. "Break," it says, "thy bread to the hungry, and those not having a roof bring into thy house." This he was doing most of all, received in his house feeding the Lord. "And if thou see one naked, cover him." This he was promising most of all, offering half his substance to all works of mercy, loosing the obligations of more violent contracts and dismissing the afflicted into release, and dissipating every unjust bond, by saying, "And if I have taken anything from anyone by calumny, I restore fourfold." And so the Lord, "Today," he says, "is salvation to this house," testified that those things were salutary which the prophet of the Creator had enjoined. But when he says, "For the Son of man has come to save what perished," I no longer contend that he has come to save what had perished, whose it had been and to whom it had perished which he had come to save; but I direct to the step of another question. That it is about man there is no doubt. He, since he consists of two substances, of body and soul, it must be inquired of what species of substance they seem to have perished. If of body, then the body had perished, the soul not. What had perished, the Son of man makes safe: the flesh therefore too has salvation. If of soul it had perished, the perdition of the soul is destined for salvation: the flesh, which did not perish, is safe. If the whole man had perished out of either substance, the whole man must of necessity be made safe, and the opinion of the heretics, denying the salvation of the flesh, is dashed. Now too the Christ of the Creator is confirmed, who according to the Creator promised the salvation of the whole man. The parable too of the servants, who are judged according to the reckoning of the lord's money lent at interest, shows God a judge, even from the part of severity, not only honouring but also taking away what one seems to have had. Or if here too he shall fashion the Creator austere, taking up what he laid not down and reaping what he sowed not, here too that one instructs me whose money he teaches me to lend at interest.

38. Christ knew whence the baptism of John was. And why did he ask as one ignorant? He knew the Pharisees would not answer him. And why did he ask in vain? Was it that out of their own mouth he might judge them, or out of their heart?
